body_en:
Business & Finance

- Prediction markets, such as Polymarket, have allowed betting on criminal cases, including the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, creating unusual challenges to the justice system. (A1)

- Amazon.com is in talks to acquire AI startup Decart in a deal that could be valued at about $7 billion. (B1)

- Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. are down by half compared with last year, but charging companies are on track to install about as many public EV plugs this year as in 2025, the industry's record high. (B1)

- United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain and his allies have claimed an easy victory in the union's election, cementing Fain's leadership of one of the most powerful forces in American organized labor. (B3)

- Jaguar has introduced the showroom-ready version of the EV it hopes will usher in a new, ultraluxury era for the British carmaker, leaving aside some of the provocative notes it sounded nearly two years ago when it announced its new strategy. (B3)

- Advertisers from Macy's to Levi Strauss have announced that a portion of the multimillion-dollar tariff refunds they received from the federal government will go to boost marketing spending as the holiday shopping season nears. (B3)

- Dutch Bros, the fast-growing, drive-through coffee chain known for its colorful drinks and outgoing baristas, has a strategy to attract pedestrian traffic: walk-up-only windows. (B3)

Worldwide

- President Trump pushed Russia and Ukraine to agree to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, as he continued to face bipartisan criticism over moves in recent days to ease U.S. pressure on Moscow and shift blame for the continued fighting to Kyiv. (A1)

- The Saudis' escalating fight with Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen is piling new challenges on the kingdom's security and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's plans to transform the country's oil-dependent economy. (A1)

- California Gov. Newsom, who has long opposed a ballot measure that would tax billionaires' wealth, is endorsing a different measure aimed at prohibiting wealth taxes. (A3)

- A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to halt any further airing of taxpayer-funded television ads touting the president, ruling they are likely illegal. (A3)

- The Justice Department is investigating whether TV networks violated antitrust laws when they briefly suspended a rotation of broadcast journalists covering the White House last month following CNN's removal from a planned assignment. (A3)

- Christa Pike, the inmate who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been discharged from the hospital and is back in prison. (A5)

- India locked down the capital in a bid to thwart a mass protest over an effort to clean up voter lists that critics say is stripping millions of the right to vote. (A9)

title: Trump's Russia Energy Deal Gets Pushback
dek: As president presses a Ukraine ceasefire, senators call his export plan illegal
byline: BY MARCUS WALKER AND ROBBIE GRAMER
body_en:
President Trump pushed Russia and Ukraine to agree to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, as the White House continued to face bipartisan criticism over moves in recent days to ease U.S. pressure on Moscow and shift blame for the continued fighting to Kyiv.

Trump on social media Sunday said there was an immediate "ENERGY CEASEFIRE" between Ukraine and Russia, despite Moscow's rejection of such a deal so far and no sign that there was an agreement in place.

The latest Trump statement came as he encountered widespread pushback on Capitol Hill to his decision to allow Russia to export oil to the U.S. and world markets and his harsh remarks toward Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky. On Sunday, a group of Democratic and Republican senators issued a joint statement calling Trump's export plan illegal and contrary to a 2022 law that banned Russian energy imports.

Trump is moving quickly to try to ease energy prices with the U.S. midterm elections just weeks away, with high gasoline and diesel prices driven by the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine conflict contributing to voter discontent toward Republicans. But analysts said the impact of new Russian supplies on lowering prices would likely be minimal.

[Continued on page A8 under the headline "Russian Oil Deal Faces Pushback":]

Russian President Vladimir Putin has rebuffed proposals for an energy ceasefire, and the Kremlin didn't respond to a request for comment. Trump previously announced such a ceasefire on Sept. 14; Russia and Ukraine continued their strikes.

Zelensky reiterated on Sunday that he is open to stopping airstrikes against Russian oil refineries if Moscow stops bombing Ukraine's energy grid, but he has staved off Trump's pressure for Kyiv to cease its strikes unilaterally. He said Ukraine's skies had been "infested" with Russian drone and bomb strikes throughout the day.

The White House didn't respond to a request for comment on the senators' statement.

Russia continued to bomb Ukraine's energy grid and other targets in Kyiv on Sunday, with explosions audible throughout the day and power cuts continuing.

"Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia does," Zelensky said in a social-media post. "We are awaiting clear details of the dialogue between America and Russia—and we expect Putin to follow through on what President Trump said."

Democrats and some Republicans have objected to Trump's efforts to ease economic pressure on Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The U.S. "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The administration must immediately reverse course," a bipartisan group of senators said in a statement on Sunday. The group is made up of Republicans Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, John Curtis of Utah and Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

The senators said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit the justification required under the 2022 law barring Russian energy imports to the U.S.

Trump's statement Sunday came after he lambasted Zelensky on Saturday, calling for his removal as Ukrainian leader and blaming him for Russia's continuing war on Ukraine—as well as for pushing up fuel prices, which have risen globally since the U.S.-Iran war disrupted Middle East energy exports.

With no end to the conflict with Iran in sight, Trump presented Russia as part of a solution, announcing a deal with Putin on Friday to boost the supply of Russian diesel to the U.S. and world markets.

Energy experts say the deal, if implemented, could benefit the Kremlin's coffers but is unlikely to provide significant relief to global energy markets.

"Our president is trying to find every answer possible," said Rep. Tom Emmer (R., Minn.) on ABC News on Sunday, defending the deal on Russian diesel.

Democrats saw it as a last-ditch effort to bring down prices ahead of the elections. "Literally, Trump has made a deal with the devil. He will do anything for Republicans to win" the midterms, said Rep. Donald Norcross (D., N.J.).

Russia has been planning to resume exports of diesel anyway, said Janis Kluge, head of Eastern Europe research at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, a think tank in Berlin. "There was no concession from Putin in this deal," he said.

Extra Russian diesel is unlikely to relieve the stress in global fuel markets. "The Middle East is much more important," he said.

Trump's comments in recent days have shown the limits of U.S. leverage in the war between Russia and Ukraine, as Europe, rather than the U.S., has become the mainstay of support for Kyiv's defense against Moscow's invasion.

Ukraine has greatly expanded domestic output of drones and other weaponry, while relying on European allies for financing and military aid. Trump has ended nearly all U.S. aid for Ukraine's defense, though the U.S. continues to share valuable satellite and other intelligence with Kyiv.

Bombing Russian refineries is the strongest card that Ukraine holds to force Putin to stop the war he launched nearly five years ago.

Russia is bombarding Ukraine's energy infrastructure in an attempt to cut off heating, electricity, water and other essential services ahead of winter. In the past week, Russia has attacked Ukraine's electricity system 196 times and its oil and gas infrastructure 20 times, Zelensky said in an interview with ABC News broadcast on Sunday.

title: Saudi Crown Prince's Burden Grows Heavier as Houthis Strike
dek: Kingdom is facing myriad dilemmas as Iran-backed rebels intensify attacks on the kingdom's security and
byline: BY SUMMER SAID AND GEORGI KANTCHEV
body_en:
DUBAI—Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman started the year on a high note. He'd just visited the White House where he was embraced by President Trump. Even after the war with Iran kicked off, Saudi Arabia looked relatively well positioned: It could export oil through a pipeline that bypassed the blocked Strait of Hormuz.

But the Saudis' escalating fight with Iran-backed Houthi militants in neighboring Yemen now piles new challenges on the kingdom's security and the crown prince's ambitious but already struggling plans to transform the country's oil-dependent economy.

On Saturday, a Houthi missile slammed into the Saudi capital's international airport, killing at least 12 people and injuring hundreds more, many seriously. It was the single deadliest attack on the U.S. or its Gulf allies in the conflicts related to the Iran war.

A 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant bled to death after her arm was blown off, one of several victims to lose limbs, officials briefed on the attack said.

Two terminals were struck and their roofs partially collapsed, people familiar with the damage said. Video verified by Storyful, which like The Wall Street Journal is owned by Dow Jones, showed passengers rolling suitcases past a trail of blood on the floor as the airport was evacuated. Authorities reported new attacks on the shuttered airport Sunday, saying a projectile caused a fire in Terminal 4 and led to injuries.

As recently as this summer, Saudi officials briefed journalists that the Houthi situation was under control. But the militants' escalating attacks, which they say are retaliation for Saudi actions against them, have hit airports and energy facilities—including the kingdom's main east-west pipeline and refineries—showing the growing threat along the southern border.

The conflict is jeopardizing Saudi efforts to build travel and tourism into a pillar of the economy, including with a marquee international investment conference scheduled for

[Continued on page A7 under the headline "Challenges Piling Up For Saudis":]

the end of the month that looks increasingly in doubt.

The costs of the war have already widened the budget deficit and threaten to push the economy into contraction.

How the crown prince handles this test will have consequences beyond the kingdom. Saudi Arabia is a major source of funding for the global tech industry and artificial-intelligence projects. It also provides basing and overflight rights to the U.S. military.

Trump told reporters over the weekend that the U.S. was in communication with the Houthis but might join Saudi strikes on the militant group.

On Sunday, a Houthi military spokesman reiterated the group's warning that Saudi airports are targets. Saudi officials said they are running low on interceptors needed to fend off further strikes.

Attacks on Riyadh—about 500 miles from Houthi territory in Yemen—have transformed parts of the Saudi capital into a battle zone, with residents taking cover as explosions ring out across the city. Debris from an intercepted ballistic missile hit a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex Thursday. Workers in the city's financial district, students at some international schools and diplomats were ordered to evacuate or take shelter.

The 41-year-old crown prince is shuttling between palaces equipped with bunkers and is guarded by a handpicked security team, officials familiar with his movements said. His last public appearance was Tuesday.

He has few good options, said Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a Persian Gulf expert and fellow with Rice University's Baker Institute. "Any military response risks getting drawn in deeper to an asymmetric conflict."

Saudi press officials didn't respond to a request for comment.

The crown prince has plowed funds over the past decade into a slate of futuristic projects with extraordinarily complex engineering requirements aimed at signaling the kingdom's modernization and drawing investment and tourism. They include the futuristic city of Neom, an enormous cube-shaped building in Riyadh and a desert ski resort. The total cost ran to the trillions of dollars—aggressive for a government with an annual budget of around $350 billion.

The costs and economic damage of war with Iran are making that already unlikely math impossible to balance.

Foreign investment fell in the first two quarters of the year and is running well behind the crown prince's 2030 target. Rising defense and infrastructure costs threaten to siphon away money needed for the economic diversification push. Even the kingdom's push to become an AI hub now carries new risks, with data centers emerging as targets.

Many of the projects pushed by the crown prince are stalled or under review.

The non-oil side of the country's economy was smaller in the second quarter than in the first, according to Capital Economics. The Saudi Finance Ministry now expects GDP to shrink by 3.6% in 2026.

The kingdom was able earlier in the year to pump oil across the desert to the Red Sea to escape Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. But in July, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, putting Red Sea shipping at risk. In September, an attack on the East-West pipeline struck at the kingdom's main escape route from Hormuz.

The crown prince got Saudi Arabia involved in Yemen's civil war in 2015, backing the country's internationally recognized government in a fight against the Houthis. It carried out airstrikes and inflamed the conflict, but also invited Houthi attacks on its oil facilities and cities including Riyadh. The sides fought to a stalemate and a ceasefire in 2022.

The new outbreak came as the crown prince was working to contain the confrontation with Iran. Attacks by Tehran early in the war demonstrated the risk to energy facilities and economic assets like airports across the Gulf. Saudi Arabia was also struggling to cover the vast country with air defense and was shifting batteries around to try to protect palaces and key energy infrastructure, people familiar with the kingdom's deliberations said. While supportive of continued economic pressure on Iran, the crown prince was telling his advisers to keep the diplomatic channel open with Iran and make clear the kingdom's intentions weren't confrontational, the people said.

The kingdom has called for help from its military ally Pakistan and is scouring the globe for air defenses, the people said. It is also looking to recruit foreign fighters to help its Yemeni allies, they said.

title: Video Cameras Are Hacked for War
dek: Combatants hijack vulnerable devices to track, surveil and attack the enemy
byline: Daniel Michaels, Anat Peled and Milàn Czerny
body_en:
As U.S. and Israeli forces bombed Iran early this year, a poultry farmer in northern Israel decided to check on his chickens. When he launched the app on his phone for the webcam outside his coop, he was alarmed to see that its language had been switched to Arabic.

He contacted Israel's National Cyber Directorate, which found that hackers had taken control of the Chinese-made camera.

They weren't interested in chickens. The camera's orientation on the coop offered it a line of sight to the movements of Israeli security forces along the nearby border with Lebanon.

The cyber directorate said it helped the farmer harden

[Continued on page A10.]

the camera's security and adjust its viewing angle to stop capturing military operations.

The farmer's webcam was one of an estimated 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras worldwide, according to cybersecurity consultants S-RM.

The devices have become a background fixture of daily life in the form of security systems, doorbells, traffic controls and even baby monitors—and potentially any of them are vulnerable to snooping, say cybersecurity experts and hackers.

“We are now seeing the conversion of civilian surveillance into wartime intelligence collection,” said Alexander Leslie, a national-security expert at threat-intelligence consultants Recorded Future, who sees a global “soft underbelly” in omnipresent digital eyeballs.

The Wall Street Journal spoke with intelligence agencies, cybersecurity experts, military officials and hackers to scope out the extent and impact of the invasive surveillance. The Journal also reviewed dozens of hours of footage and hundreds of images, much of it made public by hackers, and independently verified their authenticity, by geolocating their locations and checking for any signs of digital manipulations.

Hidden gems

Intelligence agencies scour the internet for vulnerable cameras and robotically tap in to them by testing millions of passwords. Now, AI has made it even easier to hack into them and analyze their data at scale, transforming cameras that were designed to boost safety into tools for combatants to track, surveil and attack the enemy—often surpassing the abilities of human intelligence analysts.

Algorithms digest endless reams of footage to find hidden gems and patterns for agents to monitor.

“AI changed everything,” said Kristopher Kortright, leader of Team OneFist, an international hacker group supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Russia and Ukraine have ramped up camera-hacking in their war, aiming to spy on each other, find new targets and assess damage from their attacks. Israel, long a master of digital spycraft, hacked into Iranian traffic cameras to help forces collect intelligence used in the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei earlier this year. Iran and its proxies have struck back by breaking into hundreds of Israeli webcams and security cameras that Israeli officials consider sensitive to national security, like the one on the chicken coop.

Condo association

“They can't look through binoculars” to see Israel from Iran, said Eliav Noori, a cybersecurity expert at Israel's cyber directorate. “So they take advantage of cameras that are exposed to the internet and turn them into lookout points.”

In 2024, Russian hackers commandeered residential webcams in Kyiv, including one installed by a condominium association to monitor the neighborhood.

Ukraine's security service, the SBU, said that Russia intended to use the hacked video feeds to find targets and “to adjust missile attacks on Ukraine,” refining their aim for subsequent strikes. The SBU said it has identified and secured, reoriented or blocked roughly 40,000 video cameras that posed potential security risks since Russia's 2022 invasion.

Russia's efforts extend beyond the war zone. Dutch intelligence agencies warned in July that “Russian state actors are systematically conducting digital espionage operations” by hacking into cameras across Europe. The operations aim to collect data on military transport routes, arms deliveries to Ukraine and the whereabouts of Ukrainian military personnel, the agencies said.

Cybersecurity consultants CloudSEK recently discovered an exposed server they suspect belongs to a Russian-speaking hacker that contained hundreds of webcam images of Ukrainian facilities involved in defense, government, energy and communications, plus assorted views of daily life. CloudSEK said many of the images came from locations near Ukraine's borders with NATO ally Romania.

War with Iran

Webcams are also playing an increasingly important role in the war with Iran. An Iran-linked group called Moses Staff hacked into a Jerusalem security camera to monitor the 2022 bus stop bombings by a Palestinian militant that killed two people and injured more than 20 others, Israel's cyber directorate said.

This year, Iranian-linked groups have hacked into more than 250 sensitive Israeli security cameras in incidents that pose immediate danger to national security, according to Israel's cyber directorate, more than in previous years. Compromised cameras include license-plate readers and security cameras near strategic sites and places where soldiers gather, including military outposts near the border with Lebanon.

The total number of cameras breached in Israel since the start of the Iran war is far higher, the cyber directorate said, adding that out of hundreds of thousands of cameras connected to the internet there, tens of thousands have vulnerabilities that Iranian hackers could take advantage of like default passwords.

Hacked cameras are taking over roles in targeting, damage assessments and other combat intelligence-gathering that were previously supplied by aerial reconnaissance or on-the-ground spies. Penetrating a well-placed camera can get analysts closer to targets and carries less risk than infiltrating the canniest secret agent.

Restricted areas

Video cameras operate silently, often in restricted areas. Ukraine's penetration of Russian camera feeds from unreachable locations have helped Kyiv strike Moscow's troops and infrastructure.

Early in the Ukraine war, Team OneFist watched feeds from cameras on Russia's Kerch Strait Bridge to Crimea, providing images that helped refine attack plans—including the fact that Russia had installed motion detectors underneath the bridge to thwart waterborne attacks.

Information from hacked cameras “can shorten decision cycles in exactly the way modern militaries care about,” said Recorded Future's Leslie.

While private individuals and enterprise-network managers are increasingly attuned to cybersecurity, web-connected devices like cameras may have fewer built-in protections and not be consistently monitored, patched or updated, said Xu Zou, senior vice president for cloud security services at cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks.

Information-security specialists inside companies and governments often aren't aware of connected cameras, which are frequently installed and operated by facilities managers or other non-IT teams. “Those teams have very little cybersecurity awareness and knowledge. Their job is to mount that camera, power it on, and walk away,” said Zou.

Information warfare

Palo Alto found last year that the vast majority of weakly secured internet-connected devices are webcams and digital video recorders. The company also found that video-streaming and video-conferencing equipment—ubiquitous in office buildings around the globe—are particularly vulnerable. That has made them useful for information warfare, not just military operations, said Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank.

Anti-Israeli groups, he said, use imagery from hacked cameras in propaganda videos and content. “For them it is about playing up their intelligence superiority,” he said.

Iranian-linked group Handala taunts Israelis by boasting that it can see and hear them close to home. “Have a message? Find the nearest traffic camera and talk,” Handala wrote last year on one of its websites, which has since been taken down.

In Russia, officials from the Ministry of Industry and Trade were grousing on a videoconference call earlier this year about their reliance on Chinese drone components when an unexpected voice joined in. “Colleagues, can you hear me?” the voice asked. Yes, replied the meeting leader. The intruder then asked a seemingly technical question that quickly turned obscene. “Turn it off,” the meeting leader told his colleagues, in a video later posted online by Ukrainian hackers.

‘Internet of things’

Vulnerable accessories linked into a network are among hackers' prime targets, expanding what technicians call the attack surface. Often, cameras aren't the target, but serve as the weak link in a larger hacking attempt. Ransomware group Akira tapped an unprotected webcam to get around one organization's network-security systems and extort it, S-RM reported last year. Once hackers are inside a local network, they can usually probe stored files, email accounts and other devices, including cameras.

“The Internet of Things is such a wild area that everything—whether you realize it or not—is an extension of your attack surface,” said Paul Caron, S-RM head of cyber for the Americas.

title: Prediction-Market Bets Spread to Jury Verdicts
body_en:
During the summer murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, bettors wagered more than $100,000 on the verdict. Since a deadlocked jury forced a mistrial in early September, more than $500,000 in additional bets have been placed on whether the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her children will eventually be convicted.

In Utah, a trial date hasn't been set yet for Tyler Robinson, who stands accused of killing conservative commentator Charlie Kirk at a university event last year. But even before Robinson formally entered a not guilty plea last month, more than $300,000 had been wagered on the outcome.

In both cases, the bets were available on an offshore platform run by Polymarket. The site also has hosted bets on the federal prosecution of Sean "Diddy" Combs and the government's current case against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Prediction markets are raising novel ethical concerns and insider-trading risks on everything from corporate auditing to U.S. military operations. Those headaches are now at the courthouse door, presenting particularly unusual challenges for the justice system.

"When the public treats a courtroom like a casino, due process is susceptible to corruption," said C. Melissa Owen, president of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers.

The most direct and obvious concern is the potential for jurors to bet on their own deliberations, creating financial incentives to reach particular outcomes, no matter the facts of the case.

Some court staffers are also potentially in positions to have inside knowledge of how deliberations are proceeding.

[Continued on page A6:]

The accessibility and pervasiveness of betting platforms makes the possibility of corrupting jurors a real risk, said University of Chicago law professor M. Todd Henderson.

"But there is a broader concern," he said, "that prediction markets with heavy betting could influence how jurors think about a case. If millions are wagered on the belief that a defendant will be acquitted, could that make a jury more reluctant to convict?"

"For Joe Q Juror sitting at home," Henderson said, "the question is: Is he likely to be biased as a juror if he sees the odds on Polymarket and if he sees a pundit in the paper or on TV talking about what the chances are that Tyler Robinson did it?"

Robinson's lawyers flagged the Polymarket bets to the presiding judge, arguing the wagering was a "morally dubious enterprise" that commodified death-penalty litigation.

The defense said trading volume was active during a preliminary court hearing in July, and argued that continuing to broadcast the proceedings would create pretrial publicity that was unfair to Robinson.

"The Court credits Defendant's concerns regarding jury contamination and prediction-market activity as genuine," Judge Tony Graf wrote in a ruling last month. But he allowed continued livestreaming of the proceedings and suggested that any concerns could be addressed in jury selection, including by asking potential jurors about any exposure they had to prediction markets.

Typically, markets for betting on criminal cases have been hosted on offshore platforms because prediction-market companies have wanted to avoid running afoul of U.S. rules that prohibit gambling on sensitive topics including war, terrorism and assassination.

Still, market observers say that accessing the offshore platforms isn't difficult. Rutgers University statistics professor Harry Crane said around 20% to 40% of the money bet on offshore Polymarket markets comes from inside the U.S. The study doesn't show whether that volume comes from many people making small bets or a small number of super-users, said Crane, who serves on an advisory committee to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets.

A Polymarket spokesperson said people "trade on outcomes of real-world events including legal, political and economic developments. These markets do not impact the outcomes—they reflect what market participants collectively believe will happen."

Polymarket has a data partnership with Dow Jones, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal.

At least a handful of courts are beginning to address the issue. The U.S. District Court in Chicago is updating its insider-trading policies to prohibit employees from using on-the-job information to make wagers. Judges in the district are on alert for similar concerns that might arise in jury trials, said Sean Lewis, a court spokesman. "As technology and society evolve, the court will continue to adapt its policies to safeguard the fair and impartial administration of justice," he said.

The federal trial court in Manhattan has attracted at least two notable betting markets. Between May and July of last year, Polymarket users bet nearly $798,000 on the verdict of the Diddy sex trafficking trial. Combs was found not guilty of racketeering and sex trafficking offenses but convicted of less serious charges.

Maduro is set to go on trial next year in the same court, on charges including narco-terrorism. A Polymarket offering on whether Maduro will be found guilty has attracted about $133,000 in trading volume so far. Another on whether he will serve prison time has seen more than $900,000 of activity.

title: The Sunday Scaries Are Real—And They're Getting Worse
dek: As workloads mount, people struggle to tame the pre-Monday dread spiral
body_en:
Jill Davis's official work week starts Monday morning. Unofficially, it kicks off every Sunday afternoon when, like clockwork, anxious thoughts begin seeping into her brain.

"Am I organized and ready enough? Am I prepared for this meeting?" says Davis, the chief development officer at a nonprofit. To bat the angst away, she'll often launch into work, writing emails and saving them as drafts so she doesn't disturb her colleagues. Chances are they're already fretting about work, too.

"Sunday scaries" have become such a fixture of Americans' weekends that Merriam-Webster added the term to its online dictionary last month. Its definition: a feeling of anxiety or sadness one may feel when the weekend is almost over, either because the work/school week is about to begin, there is no more time for fun or relaxing weekend activities, or both.

That pre-Monday dread isn't a new phenomenon, but there's reason to believe it's intensifying as workloads mount and job security ebbs. More than half of U.S. workers say they experience

[Continued on page A12.]

the Sunday scaries, according to an October survey of 2,100 people by job platform FlexJobs. Having a list of unfinished tasks hanging over them was the most commonly cited cause.

It's only a matter of time before the scaries ruin Saturday too, turning it into a day to dread the dread we'll feel on Sunday.

For Davis, the jitters so consumed her Sundays that she bought a $30 hourglass to rein them in. It takes an hour for the sand to run through it—the maximum time she now lets herself work, or even think about work. On a recent Sunday, “when it ran out, I got up and I left and went in the other room,” she said.

Effectively treating the Sunday scaries without causing negative side effects is a delicate balancing act. It requires being busy enough to ease the stress but not the kind of busy that drags everyone down. It appears we're getting worse at that.

The share of Sundays that employees devoted to work messaging and chats was about 12% last year, compared with 6.6% in 2023, according to data compiled for The Wall Street Journal by workforce analytics firm ActivTrak.

“People feel like they have to toil away harder in order to make sure they don't get fired,” said Angie Callen, an executive coach and author of “Scary Good: Discovering Life Beyond the Sunday Scaries.” Her advice? Ask yourself honestly why you are engaging with work on a Sunday. Will you get a positive return on your time? “You don't have to settle for the Sunday scaries,” said Callen. “We let Mondays ruin our Sundays. Stop. Be present in your life instead of accepting that default.”

Joanna Johnston, a longtime tech executive, used to combat her Sunday scaries by getting up as early as 6 a.m. to squeeze in an hour of Monday prep work, then putting in more time in the evenings. When she sent Slack and other messages, it was usually to a peer or in response to a manager. But she didn't always adhere to the unwritten rules of weekend communication with subordinates. “I'm sure before I became more sensitive to the intrusion this caused, I did it to my direct reports and broader team as well,” said Johnston, who retired from corporate roles in June and now coaches executives. Despite the career shift, she's still working on Sundays. “I think I just have a problem,” she laughed.

Until a few years ago, Chris Keller ran his own marketing agency and often worked seven days a week. Now in a corporate role, he limits himself to two hours on early Sunday mornings to prepare for the week. Otherwise, “I know it could get away from me really quickly,” said Keller, marketing chief at a credit union. Keller said he will typically use the time to dictate notes to a transcription app to prepare for meetings. “If I don't get ideas and thoughts out, I'll not be able to enjoy the other things that I'm supposed to be doing on the weekends,” he said.

Do psychiatrists approve? If doing some work on Sunday will relieve you of feeling behind or overwhelmed on Monday, it's OK, just set guardrails, said Kia-Rai Prewitt, a psychiatrist with Cleveland Clinic's Behavioral Health. “If I can just log in really quick and respond to this email, that's all I'm going to do,” she said. “You have to set the boundary and say, ‘I'm not going to respond to other emails.’”

Others recommend exhausting all options to avoid work altogether. Consider spending a little more time at work on Friday “so you can officially be done” or getting to work a little earlier on Monday “so that you're not going to be behind the eight ball,” said Amy Cooper Hakim, an industrial organizational psychologist. “There's always a way to shift those same extra minutes.”

If all else fails, try a rebrand. Davis, the Sunday afternoon worrier, worked with an executive coach who helped her reimagine the “Sunday scaries” as “Monday maybe.” The idea is to approach Monday with curiosity rather than thinking everything has to be buttoned-up and perfect by then. “I'm trying to release the pressure of what's so special about everything getting done before Monday,” she said. “I sleep better on Sunday nights.”

terms.en: Scary Good: Discovering Life Beyond the Sunday Scaries

title: Americans' Savings Help Fuel Private Credit
dek: and helped power the rise of their private lending to risky companies
body_en:
When Sabrina Elliott inherited some money, her son-in-law helped her invest $40,000 in a product that dangled the prospect of stock-market gains with no risk of loss.

In exchange for locking up her money for 12 years, it promised returns tied to the market's performance. One catch: The company behind the product, Aviva, could periodically lower the portion of market gains Elliott received.

That happened twice after Aviva was purchased by Athene, an insurer backed by private-asset giant Apollo Global Management. By the time the policy ended in late 2023, her annualized return had come to 3.7%.

"That's one of the downfalls of the indexed annuities," said Carlos Dias Jr., Elliott's son-in-law and a financial adviser outside Orlando, Fla. "Insurance companies can change the amount that's received from the particular index every year, every two years."

Wall Street behemoths like Apollo and Brookfield are just now starting to find ways to tap in to the vast sums of money in 401(k) accounts, pitching their alternative investments as another way for people to grow their nest eggs.

But private-asset managers have already been vacuuming up the savings of American households through indexed annuities, which have surged in popularity over the past decade

[Continued on page A10.]

The annuity industry recently got a black mark after Delaware Life, an insurer controlled by Dodgers owner Mark Walter, disclosed it was under federal investigation for failing to report loans to other entities he owned.

Indexed annuities are meant to appeal to older people who may be on fixed incomes and have little appetite for risk, but still want some exposure to stock-market gains. People turn over $50,000 or $100,000 worth of savings for a decade or so. Insurers guarantee that their investment return will never fall below zero, with the potential for better returns than a CD or savings account.

Exactly how much a person's money grows is based on terms the insurer can change during the life of policy, such as the share of the deposit that can earn market returns, any cap on returns and any spread subtracted from those returns.

In the first year of Elliott's policy, 60% of her money earned returns tied to the S&P 500, minus a 2.9-percentage-point spread. In the policy's seventh year, Athene lowered that share to 55%, then to 45% in the 11th year. The rest of the money grew at a fixed rate of 1%.

Elliott, a 69-year-old professor of nutrition in the Florida university system, had paid for add-ons that let her choose to parcel out payments over her lifetime or to her heirs. That reduced her annual return by about 2 percentage points.

The 3.7% annualized rate she earned over the 12-year life of her annuity beat the 1.9% she would have gotten from Treasurys. But it paled next to the annualized return of 13% on the S&P 500.

Athene, which Apollo fully took over in 2022, said in a statement that the annuity “performed exceptionally well, earning returns well in excess of similar safe yield alternatives, guaranteeing 100% principal protection, and providing optional enhanced death benefits and guaranteed lifetime income.”

The company said “it is highly misleading to measure the performance of fixed indexed annuities using a scenario that pairs historically low rates with a strong bull equity market.”

Products tied to the stock market are typically overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and selling them often requires a securities license. But indexed annuities can also be sold by state insurance agents, who aren't subject to the same rules on disclosing conflicts of interest or acting in a client's best interest. Indexed annuities are often among the most lucrative products these agents can sell.

American Equity, for instance, pays agents a commission of 5% to 7% of a policyholder's deposit on some 10-year indexed annuities. That is compared with around 3% for simpler annuities with fixed rates sold by the Brookfield-owned insurer.

Insurers say the higher commissions reflect the complexity of the products, which require greater explanation. Still, consumer advocates say indexed annuities can be a magnet for misleading sales pitches.

Educational materials for an indexed annuity sold by Delaware Life, for instance, show a premium of $100,000 growing to $2.7 million over the next 21 years. But the “Momentum Growth” annuity is tied to a stock-and-crypto index established just last year. The returns advertised draw on hypothetical data based on the past 15 years—a period that included 11 years with double-digit stock-market gains.

After the financial crisis, private-asset managers began buying up insurers to access their huge pools of policyholder premiums. Indexed annuities were particularly attractive. Payouts follow a relatively predictable timetable, and the policies typically last about a decade, compared with about three to five years for fixed-rate annuities. That gives asset managers flexibility to put the money into riskier, less-liquid private-credit investments like collateralized loan obligations or asset-backed securities.

If their investments do poorly, the insurer can cushion against loss by lowering the caps on policyholder gains, and if their investments do well they can fatten their profits the same way, said Larry Rybka, chief executive of Valmark Financial Group, which sells life insurance, annuities and investment products. “That's why private equity likes this, because they can change the deal on the consumer,” Rybka said.

title: Why Higher Bond Yields Aren’t Going Away
byline: THE OUTLOOK | By Matt Grossman and Anthony DeBarros
body_en:
Some economic shocks look like bumps in the road—tariffs, to which businesses adjust, or a war with Iran that raises oil prices temporarily. But economists increasingly believe that higher U.S. interest rates will define the rest of the decade.

So concludes The Wall Street Journal's latest survey of forecasters. The surveyed analysts don't see the recent surge in long-term yields to quarter-century highs as a temporary blip that will fade as inflation cools. Instead, they expect higher long-term yields to be sustained.

Treasurys set the tempo for borrowing costs across the economy. Higher yields mean higher mortgage rates and more expensive borrowing for companies. They also increase the burden on the federal budget, where interest on the national debt now exceeds military spending.

The 71 analysts who submitted projections in the survey from Oct. 2-7 now expect the benchmark 10-year yield to end 2026 at 5.1%, up from 4.4% the last time we asked, in July. Not all respondents answered every question.

Higher yields are expected to persist. Forecasters see a 10-year yield of 4.96% halfway through 2027 and 4.78% at the end of 2027, up from 4.3% and 4.26% in July projections.

A mix of improving growth, inflation and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory have pushed bond yields higher since the start of the summer. Many economists said the cocktail has forced them to re-evaluate assumptions about demand for Treasurys, whose yields rise when their prices fall.

"It has been a sea change in the fundamentals underlying the fixed-income market and the economy," Allen Sinai, president of consulting firm Decision Economics, said in an interview.

He said even after the Federal Reserve's interest-rate increase last month, the central bank has fallen behind in the battle to tame inflation. Sinai said it would take more than one hike to smother inflation, which the Fed appeared to acknowledge with its September projections. Those showed the Fed's short-term interest-rate target, the federal-funds rate, topping 4% this year and staying there through 2027.

Sinai forecasts the 10-year yield could rise to nearly 6% next year and remain above 5% through the 2020s. Yields on Treasury securities are heavily influenced by investors' expectations for how the Fed will set interest rates in coming years.

Much of the recent increase in inflation is because of higher oil prices, which economists expect to recede: They forecast the U.S. oil-price benchmark will end the year at $88 a barrel, compared with $91.85 on Friday, and slip below $80 by July.

As a result, they expect inflation as measured by the consumer-price index of 3.5% in December, 2.6% next June, and 2.3% at the end of 2027. That has changed little from three months ago. The inflation gauge that the Fed tracks, the personal-consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to cool to 2.4% by the end of 2027, from 3.5% at the end of this year.

Carl Tannenbaum, chief economist at Chicago-based Northern Trust, said factors beyond the inflation outlook have pushed up expected yields. Inflationary pressure from the Iran war could abate if the conflict winds down, which would help ease yields, all else equal, he said. But investors will remain nervous about the large and growing debt burden, while the AI infrastructure build-out could lift growth expectations and demand for capital, Tannenbaum said. He sees the 10-year yield around 5.2% through 2028, before falling to 5% by the end of 2029.

Yields at that level would strain the federal budget. In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected the 10-year Treasury yield won't exceed 4.3% for the rest of the decade. The White House Office of Management and Budget is even more optimistic, projecting yields falling into the mid-3% range later this decade.

Economists penciled in higher expected growth this year. They expect GDP to increase by 2.4% in 2026, up from their 2.1% July projection. That reflects upward revisions to second-quarter growth and interim data suggesting the economy might have grown by an annualized rate of more than 3% in the third quarter. Respondents see growth slipping back thereafter, to 2.1% or 2.2% for the rest of the decade.

Likewise, forecasters don't anticipate much drama in the labor market. On average, they think unemployment will hang around 4.2% through 2029, little changed from the 4.2% unemployment rate in September.

They put the probability of recession in the coming 12 months at 24%, barely budged from 25% in July.

Not all forecasters agree yields will stay high. Rajeev Dhawan, an economist at Georgia State University, thinks the labor market is more fragile than it appears.

Over the past six months, the economy has added a solid 66,000 jobs a month on average, but few have been in the most lucrative fields, he said.

In Dhawan's view, a weaker labor market could force the Fed to bring rates lower again, which could pull down yields. "The labor market's got a white-collar job malaise," Dhawan said. "Once the Fed realizes it isn't as strong, they will pivot to rate cuts."

title: Fed’s Hammack Sees Engine of Inflation on Factory Floor
body_en:
CLEVELAND—Jack Schron spent most of 90 minutes last week showing Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack how good business has gotten at Jergens, a family-run manufacturer built on the site of old railroad buildings on the city's east side.

Orders from aerospace companies are surging, tariffs have made a Chinese rival's parts more expensive, and the company is about to make the biggest machine-tool purchase in its 84-year history.

Jergens makes industrial hardware such as clamps and quick-release pins that lock everything from aircraft panels to concert speakers into position. What matters most to his customers has shifted, Schron told the central banker. Quality is still the minimum for getting in the door at the aerospace giants. "The next threshold used to be price," he said.

Now it is speed. "No one wants to wait on anything anymore," said Schron, the company's president. Buyers will pay a premium to get products in weeks instead of months, and that has helped Jergens' bottom line.

That kind of pricing power worries inflation fighters like Hammack. It suggests demand is outrunning what suppliers can make, a dynamic that higher interest rates are supposed to tamp down. Yet interest rates never came up during her visit, which ended with a tour of the busy factory floor.

Jergens is one company, but its experience fits what Hammack said she is hearing from across her district. "You heard it from Jack. He's buying expensive machinery. He's investing. He sees a lot of demand. The growth is there," Hammack said in an interview after the tour.

It is a big reason she thinks the Fed, which raised its benchmark rate last month to a range of 3.75% to 4%, needs to go higher still. With inflation above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, Hammack says she hears from lower-income households that are no longer just trading down at the grocery store but choosing which bills to pay.

Most of her colleagues last month saw inflation returning to target in 2029. "To me, that's far too long," she said.

Hammack, who spent more than 30 years at Goldman Sachs before joining the Fed in 2024, has been among the most outspoken officials in pushing for higher rates. "I grew up in a world as a trader where if I was wrong 49% of the time, that was a pretty good day, so I'm not afraid of putting out a forecast," she said.

Hammack was early to argue that rates might not be restraining the economy as much as Fed officials thought, and the boom in AI-related spending rippling through the industrial and technology sectors has since brought more of her colleagues around to that view.

The question now is how quickly to adjust. Minutes of the Fed's September meeting showed most officials thought another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end, and several have signaled they think the Fed doesn't need to raise rates again this month.

Hammack didn't sound as patient. "Smaller, more frequent adjustments are preferable to larger" ones, in part because making bigger moves can be harder for businesses to prepare for, said Hammack.

In July, when the Fed held rates steady, she was one of three policymakers who dissented in favor of a rate increase.

Officials often gauge how much they are restraining the economy against some estimate of an unobservable "neutral" rate, the level that neither spurs nor slows growth. Hammack said her estimate is among the highest on the committee, and that if she is wrong, it is too low.

"When you see the amount of capital that's flowing in, when you see the profits that are being created, to me, this does not look like an economy that has restraint," she said.

Long-term Treasury yields have been on the march since the summer, raising borrowing costs across the economy. Hammack said that has moved financial conditions closer to neutral, but she rejected the suggestion that the bond market could do the Fed's work for it. "Absolutely not," she said. "It's not a substitute, it's a complement."

Outside the Fed, critics argue that higher rates are the wrong tool for the job. They can't produce more oil and may not immediately slow AI spending financed by tech giants' cash and the bond market. Hammack conceded the point. "I do not think that raising rates is going to materially slow the data-center demand," she said.

Hammack's willingness to say where she stands sets her apart from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Warsh has said he wants to move the Fed away from signaling its own moves or narrating its forecasts, which he has argued locks officials into defending a projection instead of responding to the economy as it unfolds.

Saying less just leaves businesses and households to guess, Hammack said. Her job is to "arm the public with as much information as possible" and to "treat them like mature grown-ups."

title: Venezuelan Bribe Suspect Arrested

body_en:
A businessman wanted in the U.S. for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.

Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a onetime ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro.

title: Man Charged in Officer’s Death
dek: PHILADELPHIA
body_en:
Authorities charged Eric Lewis, 35, with homicide in the killing of a police officer Saturday, Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said.

Shane Seiber, 40, was shot and killed after responding to a report of a man with a gun, police said. An officer who was with him was shot 12 times and is in stable condition, Commissioner Kevin Bethel said.

title: Man Targets His Family, Killing Eight
dek: PENNSYLVANIA
body_en:
A man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pa., before taking his own life as well, authorities said.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims in Friday's shooting, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman.

title: Newsom Backs Bid To Counter Billionaire Tax Effort
body_en:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has opposed a high-profile ballot measure that would tax billionaires' wealth. Now he is endorsing a different measure aimed at prohibiting wealth taxes.

Newsom announced his endorsement Friday via the campaign backing the antitax measure, known as Proposition 42. "Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes," Newsom said.

Prop. 42 has raised tens of millions of dollars from a political committee funded in part by billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. This effort took off after a healthcare-workers' union proposed a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' wealth. Voters are set to decide on both ballot measures on Nov. 3.

The proposed billionaire tax, aimed at offsetting steep cuts to Medicaid funding signed into law last year by President Trump, is novel in the U.S. Unlike the income taxes that most Americans pay, it would apply to the net worth of California residents with net assets of $1 billion or more.

The wealth tax has exposed bitter divisions in the Democratic Party and in California's labor movement.

Newsom came out against the tax last year, weeks after it was proposed by a healthcare-workers union, and has argued the levy could push the state's largest taxpayers to flee. The state Democratic Party, meanwhile, voted in August to endorse the measure.

Prop. 42 could invalidate a billionaire tax by changing California's constitution to prohibit new taxes on financial assets or personal property, other than real estate.

The California Democratic Party and several large unions oppose it.

California billionaires have poured money into campaigns claiming the tax could weaken the state's fiscal base or be expanded by the legislature to apply to a broader swath of residents.

A likely legal battle looms if voters approve this measure and the wealth tax.

The union backing the billionaire tax effort—the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West—said Newsom was siding with California's wealthiest residents over healthcare for children and families. "Governor Newsom is in lock step with his billionaire-backers," Debru Carthan, the union's vice president, said.

title: Local Politics Stymie Silicon Valley Standoff
dek: between county leaders and developers frustrates $3 billion project
body_en:
SOLANO COUNTY, Calif.—In the summer of 2025, lobbyists for Silicon Valley-backed entrepreneur Jan Sramek were in overdrive. With Gov. Gavin Newsom's office in his corner, Sramek was chasing a prize: a $3 billion shipyard beside the city he wants to build from scratch here.

"WE HAVE SOME GREAT NEWS!!!!!!," a Newsom staffer emailed after the site made the shortlist. "We have not had the chance to land a WHALE of a project like this since Tesla more than a decade ago."

The excitement didn't last. Within an hour, Sramek warned of an obstacle: county government red tape. Ten months later, the shipmaker, Saronic Technologies, chose Brownsville, Texas, taking with it an estimated 10,000 jobs.

Sramek, 39 years old, is no stranger to big deals. By 22, he was handling multimillion-dollar trades at Goldman Sachs in London. Now, he is trying to build a kind of walkable suburban utopia, with housing, a high-tech manufacturing hub and a shipyard, a 90-minute drive from San Francisco. His company California Forever has raised about $1 billion from investors, including venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, assembled top urban planners and won over state leaders including Newsom.

The group wants to address a regional housing shortage around San Francisco, as well as a lack of jobs in Solano County, which this year lost a Budweiser brewery and a Valero Energy refinery.

But its biggest hurdle is the county itself.

The face of the opposition is Mitch Mashburn, 59, a cowboy-hat-wearing Republican county supervisor and descendant of local farmers who has complained the push for the shipyard was being "crammed down our throat."

Sramek casts the standoff as a fight against forces that have priced people out of housing and stalled local economies. "The battle for the future of California is being fought in Solano County," he said.

Opponents view it as a tech-billionaire land grab. "I call it broligarch city because it's really tech bros behind this," said Jim DeKloe, a community-college professor and local Sierra Club leader.

Emails seen by The Wall Street Journal show relations have soured to the point where county officials appear more inclined to block the project than negotiate.

Former County Supervisor Jim Spering faults both sides. County leaders like Mashburn aren't forward-looking and don't know how to cut deals that would help the region, he said. And Sramek is one of those "dreamer developers that don't understand that you've got to build a relationship with the community" before "telling them what you want to do," Spering said.

Sramek said he thinks his project would have faced stiff opposition no matter the approach. From the start, his campaign to buy up 60,000 acres for a master-planned community for 400,000 people enraged locals, especially after California Forever sued multigenerational farming families, alleging they conspired to inflate land prices. He called opponents the "70-year-old Sierra Club type."

Afterward, Sramek and Mashburn pledged to slow down and work together. The detente faced its first test in Saronic's planned large shipyard along the Sacramento River on California Forever's land. As Saronic, which makes autonomous sea vessels, weighed sites in 2025, Sramek's deputies courted local leaders with riverside tours alongside retired military brass.

But by April, county officials were feeling sidelined. When a Sramek deputy reminded then-County Administrator Bill Emlen of six months of meetings with him, Mashburn and others, receipts attached, Emlen shot back. "Sending invites to public briefings does not substitute for a seat at the table," he wrote.

Sramek found an ally in Bret Prebula, a former government and restless dealmaker who became city manager of Suisun City, one of Solano County's poorest communities. Prebula, 43, saw an opportunity for his 4-square-mile city, which has a large Black population and has long felt overlooked in Solano County. In early 2025, he proposed expanding Suisun City's borders by 35 square miles to annex a significant portion of California Forever's land. For Prebula, it meant city revenue. For Sramek, it was a way around the county's strict rules on development outside city limits.

In June 2025, Sramek offered Suisun City a $55,000 grant for the local July 4 fireworks celebration and other events threatened by a budget shortfall. He offered to buy $1.5 million in downtown properties to help close the gap, emails show.

Soon after, they struck a deal: California Forever would cover the city's project-related costs and pay it $10 million if the annexation is finalized.

Opponents cried foul. DeKloe, the Sierra Club leader, called it a "weasel tactic" intended to bypass a county-wide vote.

When Solano County made the shortlist last August, Sramek pushed for special legislation to fast-track the project. State lawmakers worked up a bill but wanted the county to sign off. At a board meeting, Mashburn chastised California Forever for the rush but voted to endorse a compromise bill.

The bill fell short for Saronic, according to Sramek. Despite months of talks between Sramek's team, Mashburn and lawmakers, trying to hammer out a better one, Saronic said in June it had picked Texas.

"We kept raising our hand and saying, if we don't pass the legislation, they are going to go to Brownsville," Sramek said, "but there wasn't the political will to get it done." A Saronic spokeswoman didn't respond to requests to comment.

Pulling into California Forever's unmarked office, Sramek called the vote a speed bump. But the emails show California Forever boosters fear Mashburn has another bullet in the chamber. The Suisun City annexation requires a tax-sharing agreement with Solano County, one developers [say] Mashburn has said publicly the county can't be forced to make.

"What's happening here is not just local friction," Prebula complained in an email to state officials. "it is a clear example of how counties can weaponize process and inertia."

title: Pro-Trump Ads Funded by Taxpayers Ordered Off the Air
body_en:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to halt any further airing of taxpayer-funded television ads touting the president, ruling they are likely illegal.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon in New York issued a four-page order late Sunday that barred the administration from using government funds to distribute the ads.

The judge, a Biden appointee, said it must cancel "any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements."

The order applied immediately to any ads scheduled to run later on Sunday night, but it wasn't immediately clear whether the ruling kept any additional ads off the air.

The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.

The Justice Department in a weekend filing said the ad buy was slated to end on Sunday.

The ads, which predominantly feature the president and promote the administration's policies, started airing on national television in September. They were paid for by federal funds from the Department of Homeland Security.

President Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in their creation, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

The judge's ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by plaintiffs including the advocacy group Common Cause and a Democratic candidate running for office in Alabama.

They argued the expenditures were used for purposes not authorized by Congress and violated restrictions on using public funds for political propaganda. "There is no legal justification—and no precedent—for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the plaintiffs said in response to the ruling.

The president said last week that he plans to pay for the controversial ads using funds from his MAGA Inc. super PAC rather than the federal government.

title: DOJ Probes Networks on Halting Coverage
byline: BY JOE FLINT AND DAVE MICHAELS
body_en:
The Justice Department is investigating whether major TV networks violated federal antitrust laws when they briefly suspended a rotation of broadcast journalists covering the White House last month following CNN's removal from a planned assignment.

Networks learned of the probe Friday, with Justice Department officials seeking records of communication among them regarding the pool, people familiar with the matter said.

Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News are part of a group of reporters, videographers, photographers and technicians who cover President Trump when he travels or when events take place in spaces that are too small for the entire press corps.

When CNN was taken out of the rotation for Trump's trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly in September—days after Trump banned the network, MS NOW and Politico from the White House—the TV pool briefly halted some coverage of the president.

"Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events."

"Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," Justice Department spokeswoman Emily Covington said. "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.

The Justice Department's investigation further escalates tensions between the Trump administration and the media. Trump said in July that ABC and NBC should lose their broadcast licenses for not carrying his speech on alleged election fraud on their networks.

He has also called unfavorable coverage treasonous, and his administration has subpoenaed journalists and limited access to government spaces.

"Summoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

Fox News parent Fox Corp. and Wall Street Journal parent News Corp share common ownership.

title: Rogue Anthropic Model Shared Fake Murder Tip
byline: BY GEORGIA WELLS AND JOSEPH PISANI
body_en:
Rogue AI models have hacked companies and tried to break into government websites. Now one has submitted a fake tip for an unsolved crime.

Police in Philadelphia say Anthropic alerted them last week that one of its artificial-intelligence models submitted a false homicide tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com.

Anthropic said the fake tip was among a group of rogue actions the company uncovered recently. The rogue activity also involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels.

The company said it has briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.

"While these cases had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful," Anthropic said.

The incident happened in July. Anthropic didn't realize it until September.

The Philadelphia Police Department said, "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

title: At Davos, Guilfoyle Boasted About Perks
dek: On a recording, ambassador said businessmen paid for her luxury travel
byline: By Rebecca Ballhaus, Joe Parkinson, Drew Hinshaw and Dana Mattioli
body_en:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, as America's newly minted ambassador to Greece, boasted at Davos about her ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her high-rolling trips around the world.

According to people who heard the conversation and an audio recording reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, Guilfoyle was flexing her connections to wealthy Greek businessmen in January as she made an urgent request. She was being blocked from attending an upcoming dinner being held for Eric Trump, and she wanted to enlist an American businessman who was on the guest list to help get her in the door.

"You know, I can deliver the world to you. Which you deserve," she said, according to the recording. "I'm going to make you a lot of f—ing money," she said at another point in the exchange with the businessman.

She expressed fury at not being on the list for the dinner, which was being organized by Greek House Davos. "You don't have the f—ing U.S., you know, ambassador to Greece not come. She should be kissing my f—ing ass," Guilfoyle said of the event's organizer.

In the end, Guilfoyle was able to score a last-minute seat. The chairwoman of Greek House Davos, Irene Vantaraki, said that her team "had to manage a small crisis [that] affected a number of high-profile guests" and that "some were disappointed." Guilfoyle was "gracious and discreet" and left the dinner early, she said.

Guilfoyle had flown to the January 2026 World Economic Forum on a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of the Greek construction company Aktor Group, she acknowledged on the recording.

Governments from Bulgaria to Albania were encouraged by Guilfoyle to do business with Exarchou and buy billions of dollars of American natural gas from his company, the Journal has reported. The Greek businessman was, she said in the recording, "my people."

He wasn't the only businessman facilitating Guilfoyle's travels. She was also planning to fly later that month to and out of Paris, on a jet with a Greek shipping tycoon, Nikolas Tsakos, to attend his wife's fashion show, she said in the recording. They had spent part of the holiday season together in the exclusive ultraluxury Swiss resort of Gstaad. "I see him every f—ing day," she said. "I'm flying with him to Paris. I'm with him this week.… He spent Christmas with him. OK? Gstaad. Like, everywhere."

When the ambassador checked in to Paris's Four Seasons Hotel George V—a favorite hotel of Hollywood A-listers and African and Middle Eastern leaders—the bill fell to Nikos Tsakos, CEO of Tsakos Energy Navigation, according to people familiar with the matter.

Guilfoyle, dressed in several designer gowns, would post photos of herself—including two with Tsakos—at the event to her 2 million Instagram followers.

Tsakos's financing of her travel hasn't been previously reported. Tsakos and his wife didn't respond to requests for comment.

Aktor Group, through lawyers, declined to comment. The lawyers for Aktor have said Guilfoyle wasn't improperly promoting Aktor's commercial interests.

A spokesman for the U.S. Embassy in Athens said the ambassador's "career in public service is guided by deep and abiding values" and that she had "faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines."

"The unsubstantiated claims are simply a distraction from the great work she is doing in Greece and the broader Eastern Mediterranean," the spokesman said.

The new revelations come as top Trump administration officials are deliberating what to do about an ambassador who was once set to marry into the first family, yet is now evolving into a political liability ahead of the 2026 midterms. Administration officials are discussing whether she should be removed, and a decision is expected by President Trump soon, aides said.

The State Department's inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received gifts or favors from private businessmen, a person familiar with the matter said.

On Wednesday, the Journal first published text messages showing Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to send $100,000 to her American Express account, and in return offered help in getting the Trump administration to look into the donor's personal tax and legal issues. A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages but declined to provide specifics.

"I just heard about it. It's too bad," Trump told reporters of the reporting on Guilfoyle as he left the White House on Friday. "I mean, I know. She's an ambassador. She was always very nice."

Last week, Guilfoyle came under fire from Democrats on Senate and House foreign affairs committees, who urged the State Department to review her conduct after the Journal investigation revealed the ambassador's efforts to promote Aktor, the Greek firm whose CEO had flown her to Davos.

The revelations have been a disruption for the White House and State Department. Guilfoyle spent several days reaching out to people in and around the administration, denying that she had sent the texts soliciting credit-card relief, and seeking their support.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio learned about her text messages from the Journal's request for comment as he was on a plane to Athens, where he would deliver a speech standing before the Acropolis, "on whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world." Aides were frustrated and feared the revelations would overshadow Rubio's marquee address, according to people familiar with the discussions. Guilfoyle joined Rubio for multiple events during his visit. Yet as Rubio departed Athens on Thursday, he declined to discuss the text messages reported by the Journal. "We don't conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story," he told reporters. Guilfoyle was on the tarmac to see him off.

Vice President JD Vance, asked about the Journal's reporting on Friday, declined to take a stance. "These are accusations," he said. "Let's see what the truth is. And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences."

Some former Trump officials expressed skepticism that Guilfoyle would face consequences. Stephanie Grisham, first lady Melania Trump's former spokeswoman, wrote in a post on X: "She knows far too much about the Trump family/inner circle & I imagine they like her as far away as possible. An angry KG stateside would not be a good thing for Trumpworld."

In recent days, congressional Democrats have intensified their calls for Guilfoyle to face an investigation or be ousted from her role—or both. In a letter to Guilfoyle on Friday, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D., N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called for an "immediate investigation" into whether the ambassador had violated federal bribery and public corruption laws. Meeks also requested the State Department inspector general investigate whether Guilfoyle had violated federal law, department regulations or ethics requirements. California Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, in a letter to Guilfoyle on Thursday said the reported conduct "raises serious public corruption and national security concerns" and requested she provide financial records and copies of her communications with certain government officials.

title: Harris’s Husband Has Reservations On Her Potential Presidential Run
byline: By Jessica Toonkel, Emily Glazer and Ken Thomas
body_en:
As former Vice President Kamala Harris lays the groundwork for a potential third presidential campaign, her husband Doug Emhoff has privately told some people he would prefer she didn't run and some donors have told her directly that a bid would be a long shot, said people familiar with the conversations.

Harris has said she is undecided on whether to launch another run for the White House, but she has taken steps that could be a precursor to such a bid, including speaking with major donors, hiring staff and traveling to battleground states to boost Democratic candidates in the November midterm elections.

Publicly, she has said she remains focused on the midterms, in which Democrats hope to win control of the House and Senate and pick up several gubernatorial seats. "I have not decided if I'm going to run again," Harris said at a NAACP event in Michigan last month as the audience gave her a lengthy standing ovation. "I do sincerely believe '28 won't matter if we don't get through '26."

Some people who have known and worked with Harris are skeptical she will mount another run.

A spokesman for Harris declined to comment.

Many Democrats, including some who remain close to her, think the party needs to put forward a fresh candidate in the 2028 election. Unlike in 2024, when the party coalesced around Harris in the aftermath of Biden's exit, she is expected to face a crowded field if she were to run again.

Emhoff is among those who have shared concerns with others about another run, though close to him expect he will support her if she decides to run.

In "107 Days," her memoir of the 2024 campaign, Harris describes her husband as protective and supportive, noting that when she was chosen to be Biden's running mate in 2020, "he made a huge sacrifice gladly and without bitterness." She wrote, "he knew it was essential that there be no appearance of conflicts of interest in our new roles. So that was his last day at his law firm."

She writes that in October 2024, "the attacks on me, and the many personal assaults he'd been experiencing were finally taking a toll." She describes an argument they had and Emhoff telling her, "We can't turn on each other," he said. She wrote, "With the hits coming from every direction, we had to stay united."

Since leaving Washington, Emhoff has returned to work as an attorney in Los Angeles at white shoe law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP.

Some of Harris's recent moves have made some donors uneasy about her intentions, some of the people said. In the weeks leading up to the midterms, Harris has appeared at private fundraisers in California including an event in Santa Monica for Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the party's nominee for governor of Wisconsin, and another for Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, the Democratic nominee for governor of Nevada.

She also joined a get-out-the-vote call with the Democratic National Committee recently, urging more than 2,000 volunteers listening live to knock on doors and engage with voters to flip seats in a dozen states across the country. "Hard work is good work," Harris said.
