title: Hegseth Gets Heat Over Livestream Firing Squad
byline: BY LARA SELIGMAN AND YOKO KUBOTA
body_en:
The planned Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan, a former Army officer who killed 13 people in a 2009 attack, has sparked a national debate after the Pentagon announced that his death by firing squad would be livestreamed.

When asked about the livestream, President Trump told reporters Friday afternoon that his administration "is making a determination about that, but he will be killed."

Nidal Hasan was a U.S.-born Muslim and Army psychiatrist working at Fort Hood in Texas who said he opened fire because he was trying to defend fellow Muslims. According to testimony, Hasan walked into a crowded building at Fort Hood on Nov. 5, 2009, with 420 rounds of ammunition stuffed in his pockets and paper towels to muffle the sound of the bullets. He yelled "Allahu akbar"—Arabic for "God is great"—and methodically shot at soldiers, repeatedly shooting wounded soldiers as they tried to escape. Hasan was eventually shot and paralyzed from the waist down in the attack. He killed 13 people and wounded 32 more.

Hasan admitted during his court-martial that he carried out the shooting because he believed the military was at war with Islam. During the trial, he acted as his own lawyer and offered no defense for the attack. He was sentenced to death in 2013 by a jury of fellow officers.

Hasan has since been held on death row at the military prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan. The Army, which is required to provide him legal counsel, declined to comment on his behalf.

It would be the first execution of a servicemember in 65 years. Only a president can approve the execution of U.S. servicemembers, who are subject to the military's own legal system. Trump approved Hasan's firing squad execution on Oct. 2 upon Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said.

Army regulation says the execution must take place no sooner than 60 days and no later than 150 days after the president's approval. In the case of Hasan, his Dec. 3 execution would be almost immediately after the 60-day mark.

If carried out as planned, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961, when U.S. Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Leavenworth after a court-martial convicted him of rape and attempted murder. It also would be the first military death by firing squad since World War II, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

"It hadn't been since World War II since we've done that. Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was: 'win,' " Hegseth said.

Hegseth said the execution was planned to take place at Fort Hood on the same day of the week and time of day that Hasan opened fire there.

Democrats and some Republicans have recoiled at Hegseth's plan to livestream the execution, with one Republican saying it turns the event into entertainment and others suggesting it puts America on par with "jihadists." Hasan had told military officials he hoped to become a martyr.

Vice President JD Vance on Friday questioned whether the livestream would happen. If it did, he said, he wouldn't be watching. "I don't know that's actually going to happen," he told reporters. He later added: "Look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it."

Bishops called on the Pentagon to reconsider the plan. "This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death," Archbishop Paul S. Coakley said. The president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called on the Pentagon to reconsider the plan.

Republicans expressing opposition include Rep. Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania, who wrote on X that the focus shouldn't be "turning an execution into entertainment." Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia, who noted he supports the death sentence, said on X: "Livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that." Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth in a post on X to reconsider, writing that, "Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."

The Pentagon and Army have declined to say where the video will be livestreamed and whether it would be put on the internet or a closed circuit for select members of the public to view. Under Army regulations, no one under the age of 18 is allowed to witness an execution of a U.S. servicemember. That rule would be impossible to follow if the military livestreams the execution on the internet.

title: Pike Out Of Hospital Following Botched Execution
body_en:
Christa Pike, the Tennessee inmate who survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection, was discharged from the hospital and is back in prison, her attorneys said.

Pike, who is 50, returned Saturday to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, where she has been for more than 30 years. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery," Pike's attorneys said.

Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, was rushed to a local hospital following the botched execution Sept. 30. Pike received two doses of pentobarbital, a sedative that at least 17 states use for capital punishment, but the execution was called off after she was still alive following the two injections.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed established protocol and that the drug has been effective. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, has since halted executions in the state.

At the hospital, Pike was at first intubated and put on a ventilator as hospital staff worked to clear the pentobarbital from her system. In recent days, Pike's attorneys said she was conscious and speaking.

Her legal team has called on the governor to commute her death sentence and allow her to live the rest of her life in prison.

title: Probe of Trump Foes Falters
dek: Departures, infighting, inexperience beset DOJ inquiry into alleged conspiracy
byline: By Sadie Gurman, Dave Michaels and Josh Dawsey
body_en:
Last year, Justice Department officials said an investigation would unravel a grand conspiracy by a cabal of national security officials who sought to undermine President Trump.

Trump allies hoped it would confirm what they have been alleging for years: Officials who investigated the president over the past decade engaged in what was essentially a coordinated effort to violate his civil rights.

Instead, the probe has been beset by departures, infighting and inexperience. The 81-year-old Reagan-era prosecutor coaxed out of retirement to lead the effort, Joe diGenova, quit last month, saying top department officials were pressuring the team to bring criminal cases before they were ready. He hadn't charged anyone. Officials denied pressuring him.

DiGenova was one of several overlapping supervisors of the probe, with different interests and marching orders, adding to the chaotic nature of the effort. Last month, another senior counsel, Kurt Olsen, who had joined the probe from the White House, resigned from the inquiry, people familiar with the matter said. He had recently lost a security clearance after failing government polygraph tests about his foreign contacts. Olsen said the security clearance issue wasn't a factor in his departure but declined to elaborate.

Trump is frustrated by the lack of progress and has complained about it to allies, a person familiar with the conversations said.

A number of the Justice Department officials said the case is proceeding apace, with roughly a dozen prosecutors continuing to pursue a set of related investigations that could result in charges in coming weeks. But they privately acknowledge the idea of tying all those loose threads together in one big conspiracy case in South Florida, as they had initially attempted, isn't a practical approach.

One of the officials said leadership is still confident in the people who continue to work on the inquiry, and recently brought on two former prosecutors. A White House spokeswoman said Trump has full confidence in Attorney General Todd Blanche to hold people accountable.

In addition to the departures of Olsen and diGenova, Justice Department officials came to believe a third supervisor of the case, Miami U.S. attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, wasn't appropriately managing the investigation and his office more broadly.

A number of the prosecutors on the probe complained to senior officials in Washington that Quiñones had given them no guidance, some of the people said.

Lawyers in the deputy attorney general's office are now directly overseeing the Florida-based investigation from Washington, officials said.

A spokeswoman for Quiñones defended his record on the job and said he was proud to serve in the Trump administration but declined to comment on the conspiracy investigation.

The putative targets of the probe include a raft of people Trump has long disdained, including former CIA Director John Brennan, former FBI Director James Comey and officials involved in the August 2022 search of his Mar-a-Lago home. (Comey was separately charged in connection with a photo he posted of seashells that Trump alleged was threatening, and a judge dismissed a second case targeting him. He has denied the charges and said the cases were an attempt at political retribution.)

The investigation, which officials informally referred to as the grand-conspiracy probe, sought to tie together a series of past episodes, including the 2016 intelligence community assessment that Russia interfered in that year's election to boost Trump; the FBI's subsequent investigation into alleged Trump campaign ties to that Russian meddling; and the more recent criminal prosecutions by special counsel Jack Smith in 2023 and 2024 that stemmed from Trump's 2020 election loss.

The probes went to two other U.S. attorneys before Quiñones raised his hand to oversee it, people familiar with the assignment said.

One of the investigation's first targets: congressional testimony Brennan had given in 2017 and 2023 about the 2016 assessment. A veteran national-security prosecutor working on that line of inquiry, Maria Medetis Long, soon told senior officials she hadn't found a basis to indict Brennan, some of the people said. In April, she was removed from the probe.

The Justice Department had struggled to find and retain other prosecutors to work on it and brought on temporary hires; some of them had never worked as federal prosecutors. The office had to give them a crash course on presenting evidence to grand juries, some people familiar with the probe said.

Justice Department officials in Washington at the time wanted prosecutors to speed up their process, including by subpoenaing witnesses to testify directly before a grand jury, without any FBI interview first, they said.

Prosecutors usually avoid doing that to make sure they know what to expect a witness to say and avoid surprises before the grand jury. Prosecutors had to later withdraw the subpoenas after realizing information the witnesses would need to discuss with grand jurors was classified.

Prosecutors had been trying to make the case that the FBI's court-authorized August 2022 search of Trump's Mar-a-Lago home, which led to charges that he illegally retained classified information, was unlawful. But an FBI agent told diGenova that tying the search to a broader conspiracy spanning from Florida to Washington would be challenging; diGenova disagreed and called FBI Director Kash Patel, who moved the agent off the investigation.

title: Air Travel Thrust Into Front Lines of War
dek: Governments caution on flying to Saudi Arabia after Houthi airport strike
body_en:
Commercial air travel has been dragged into the front lines of escalating conflicts across the globe, with airports, planes and airspace becoming the deliberate target of missile and drone attacks on a scale not seen before.

Since the U.S. and Israel started the Iran war in February, major airports across the Middle East have been repeatedly targeted. Parked aircraft have been hit by missiles or falling debris from interceptor systems, killing crew members and passengers.

The threat culminated Saturday in a Houthi missile strike at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300 others. The strike, the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade, left airlines scrambling to divert scores of aircraft and cancel more than 1,000 other flights. Authorities reported new attacks on the closed airport Sunday, saying a projectile caused a fire in Terminal 4 and led to injuries.

Governments including the U.S., U.K. and Australia are telling citizens to avoid the Riyadh airport following the attack. France, Canada and Germany are warning airlines that flying over all or large parts of Saudi Arabia is no longer safe.

Experts and safety advocates say travelers shouldn't take an airline's decision to fly as a guarantee of a route's safety. "All of this is up to the individual country managing its airspace, and the airline to conduct its own risk assessment," said Matt Borie, chief intelligence officer at aviation security specialist Osprey Flight Solutions. "They're counting on the country to have done the right things to keep the airspace safe," he said.

Since late February, Iran has blown up fuel tanks and damaged parked aircraft, runways and air-traffic control infrastructure across major airports in Dubai, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and elsewhere.

Israeli strikes have meanwhile hit targets at Beirut Airport, while Saudi Arabia bombed Yemen's San'a Airport in July to prevent a plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing.

The increasing threat to civilian aircraft has prompted rare rebukes from the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations body that governs global air travel, which last month reiterated a call for member states to prevent aviation from being dragged into ongoing hostilities.

The warnings over Saudi Arabian skies, which had been regarded as one of the few safe passages through the Middle East, are pushing airlines to scale back flying in what had become one of only two primary corridors linking Europe and Asia. Airlines have repeatedly had to alter flight paths to account for global conflicts, with the rapidly shrinking airspace proving painful at a time when jet fuel is trading at about twice the price it was this time last year.

The shifts began in earnest with the closure of Ukrainian skies in early 2022 and Moscow's subsequent ban on European, U.S. and other carriers using its skies. The closure of a critical corridor over Iraq at the start of the Iran war this year pushed more airlines to fly through Saudi airspace. Increasingly, airlines have been relying on a sliver of airspace passing over Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan to travel between Europe and Asia. Virgin Atlantic, for example, has been flying its twice-daily route from Mumbai to London via central Asia since late September. The airline previously routed it frequently through Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

Carriers often are left with no good options. Air India and Turkish Airlines have shifted some routes so that their aircraft fly along the Saudi-Iraq border further away from threats of Houthi attacks. But those flight paths typically pass near Syria's capital, Damascus, which is still regarded as a risky zone.

title: Pope Plans Surgery To Remove Nodule
dek: VATICAN
body_en:
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery "in the coming days" to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate.

The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week.

The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. The Vatican didn't say when the surgery would take place.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan, according to the American Cancer Society. If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said.

Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.

title: Villages Evacuated Amid Flash Flood
dek: NEPAL
body_en:
Residents along the Budhi Gandaki river in north central Nepal evacuated Sunday as flash flooding destroyed homes and other structures in the area.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority evacuated villagers and warned others to move to safer areas while remaining on alert until late Sunday.

The agency said at least five people are reported missing. The flood also damaged or destroyed four bridges, swept away about three dozen houses and damaged the construction site of a hydropower plant. Several power and communication towers were also damaged along the riverside.

Nepal's army was continuing to rescue stranded people using helicopters and ground troops. They had rescued 49 people by Sunday afternoon.

The agency said the flash flood was caused by a landslide that blocked the Budhi Gandaki river near the village of Chumchure. The dam formed by the landslide breached, triggering the flood.

The Budhi Gandaki river merges into the Trishuli river and is a key waterway near the capital Kathmandu.

title: Arrest Made in Plot To Attack Tusk
dek: POLAND
body_en:
A man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country's interior minister said Sunday.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned.

Poland has been on high alert following a recent series of school stabbings, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion.

"The man who threatened an attack was detained," Tusk wrote on X. "Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action."

Poland's police had said earlier on Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

"We take this matter extremely seriously," said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland's intelligence services. He said authorities considered there was a "high probability" the threats would be carried out.

title: New Delhi Locks Down As Voter Protests Grow
byline: BY TRIPTI LAHIRI AND KRISHNA POKHAREL
body_en:
NEW DELHI—The government of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi locked down India's capital with thousands of security forces in a bid to thwart a mass protest over an effort to clean up voter lists that critics say is stripping millions of Indians of the right to vote.

Last year, India's election commission began a cleanup of voter lists that, according to activists, have resulted in some 130 million people being cut from preliminary or final voter rolls.

Modi's government and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party have said the cleanup—the first in two decades—was needed to preserve the integrity of the lists and remove deceased, duplicate or fraudulent voters, such as illegal immigrants they say have entered from India's eastern border with Bangladesh.

The anger over the voting lists has melded with grievances from young Indians struggling to find work, together presenting a stiff challenge to Modi.

A youth movement called the Cockroach Janta Party emerged in the spring following a scandal over a university entrance exam. The group has thrown its support behind those protesting the voting issue, joining in Saturday's protests in New Delhi.

In the Indian capital, police—who were deployed starting before dawn—stopped vehicles and pedestrians at yellow metal barricades. Dozens of metro stations were closed and many intercity trains were canceled.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach party, posted a video of himself and fellow protest leaders being taken into custody on their arrival at New Delhi's airport. "This is dictatorship," Dipke shouted as the police officers entered the plane.

Wall Street Journal reporters saw about 100 people being detained over the course of two hours.

Over the course of the day, thousands were detained in the capital, according to Cockroach party activists and multiple local news accounts. The Journal couldn't independently verify the numbers. A Delhi police spokesman didn't respond to requests for comment.

Dipke and his two fellow activists were released following a court appearance Sunday.

On Saturday, Ishrat Ansari, 49, said she set off at dawn from her home in the north of the capital, walking 9 miles to reach the protest area.

She said she, her son and her daughter received notices this year from election authorities that their names had been flagged for discrepancies. In her case, she thinks it was because her name appeared on 2002 voter rolls with the honorific "Khatun," often used by Muslim women, which doesn't appear on her current identification. The social worker, who mainly goes by her first name, feared that she may have received the notice because she is a Muslim. "Is it because my name is Ishrat that I was cut?"

Modi's BJP has promoted a form of Hindu nationalism that his critics say discriminates against India's Muslim minority. The government denies that, and says its policies are focused on the progress of all Indians.

title: Kenyan Club Rejects Bid To Allow Women Into Bar
body_en:
One of Kenya's most prestigious social clubs has voted to keep women out of its men-only bar for the foreseeable future.

The policy, reflected in a fictional scene where Meryl Streep's character is coldly turned away in the 1985 film "Out of Africa," has spurred rancorous debates at the exclusive club for months and was the subject of an article in The Wall Street Journal earlier this year.

Muthaiga Country Club in Nairobi, opened in 1913 for the British elite, has evolved into an exclusive club for top government officials, wealthy businesspeople and successful professionals. Membership is by invitation only, with admission fees upward of $4,000.

Yet its century-old Member's Bar has remained strictly reserved for men, and women can only go in once or twice a year during major club events.

For some members, the bar policy is a source of frustration that has been simmering for decades. For others, it is "hallowed ground in terms of the genesis story of the club."

More than 700 club members voted on Thursday to keep the men-only bar and set up a separate space for women, against 200 who supported the idea of opening up the men's bar to everyone. "It was a slaughter," said one male member, who had to follow events from outside because the ballroom, where the vote happened, was packed. Over 1,000 members followed the meeting online.

The club didn't respond to a request for comment.

One female member opened the debate by defending the men's bar as one of the few remaining spaces men could be men, and insisted that the club had bigger fish to fry than the bar, members recounted. Another woman member who had been campaigning against the men's bar suddenly decamped to the other side.

Other members, including many women, argued that they shouldn't have to pay for the running of a bar they couldn't use.

Some members worry the vote could jeopardize reciprocal privileges with over 100 affiliated international clubs. London's Reform Club already ended its agreement over the policy, and an American club recently withdrew its interest in having a reciprocal arrangement, members familiar with the matter said.

Chloé Spo, the French businesswoman who resubmitted the proposal to open up the bar to all members, concluded that Muthaiga is "still a man's club."

title: Hoping to Land Next Summer’s $50,000 Internships? Too Late
dek: Elite financial firms are recruiting earlier and paying handsomely for prospective talent
body_en:
The school year is barely a month old, but for college students hoping to land a primo internship next summer it might already be too late. Elite financial firms that pay around $50,000 for 10-week programs have been recruiting for weeks, if not months. While most of their peers are still decorating their dorm rooms, hard-charging undergrads are vying for these coveted seats. Some already have offers for 2027 or are deep in the interview process. And just as students are in a frenzied competition with one another, firms such as Citadel, Five Rings and Jane Street Capital are hustling to lock down the most promising talent before their rivals do. In this arms race, 20-year-olds now command pay rates that most Americans don't reach at the peaks of their careers, never mind as interns.

“When I got the offer call and they said how much the salary was, I asked a few times if they were saying the right number,” says Karthik Kallam, fresh off a quantitative-trading internship at Susquehanna International Group. “I can't fathom how an intern should be making that much money.”

Top internship programs have long been competitive, but those dangling stratospheric compensation rates now have acceptance rates of less than 1%. You'd have a better chance of getting into Harvard. The result is that application cycles keep starting earlier. Some firms now open applications for the following summer's internships while the current cohort is still on the job. Starting early affords time for multiple rounds of interviews. These culminate in on-site “super-days” where evaluators gauge whether candidates are as impressive in person as they seemed on-screen—and don't have access to AI.

The most selective financial firms are often looking for a kind of raw intelligence that doesn't show up on students' transcripts. They sometimes scout collegiate chess and poker tournaments, looking for people who are uncannily good at playing the odds and anticipating what will happen next. Kallam plays both games competitively. He says he believes his prowess at the table did more to boost his internship application than his sparkling GPA at Ohio State, where he is studying computer science and statistics. Then there is the quant factor. In quantitative finance, where many of the highest-paying internships are concentrated, experience arguably matters less than in most other disciplines.

If you were choosing a personal-financial planner, you'd want someone with decades' worth of judgment and intuition—a pro with a steady demeanor that comes from having seen it all before. Quant traders don't necessarily need that. They use mathematical models to predict where markets are going and take pride in removing emotion from investment decisions. “They can become exceptional very quickly because of their technical skills and the opportunities we give them,” says John Talarico, global head of talent acquisition at Millennium Management, though he adds that experience is a plus. In this way, finding promising talent for niche finance roles is a bit like scouting athletes. A college quarterback may not know how to read an NFL defense or have any experience in a professional team's style of play. Yet coaches might see potential in his arm strength and decision-making. Similarly, firms like Millennium might see an upside in candidates who have never taken a finance course. If their logic, problem solving and pattern recognition are off the charts, then they could become major moneymakers. To find out whether they have what it takes, it's worth paying them handsomely for the 10-week equivalent of training camp. At this level, interns aren't fetching coffee; they are auditioning for full-time jobs with base salaries around $300,000. With so much at stake, shenanigans are inevitable.

“Always say you're a junior” is the unofficial motto of students applying for top-flight financial internships, a former Arrowstreet Capital intern told me. The thinking is that third-year college students are the most appealing because they are close to graduation. Sophomores and freshmen sometimes fudge their class years in hopes of improving their chances.

And I thought college students only lied about their ages to get into bars.

Their deception is laced with desperation. A lot of high-achieving students have an unhealthy fear of falling behind, says Joe Catrino, executive director of the Dartmouth Center for Career Design. “It's a troubling thing for us because we see students that have this anxiety and stress that they have to figure out what they want to do, and they just got here,” he says. At Ivy and other top colleges, this often results in a frenzied effort to gain acceptance into selective clubs on campus almost as soon as first-year orientation wraps up. Membership promises a standout résumé line, as well as access to peer and alumni networks. Ishaan Shah recalls being rejected by the quantitative-trading club at Penn in his first semester of college. He applied again in the spring semester—and was turned down once more. The third time was the charm. Being in the quant club helped propel him to an internship at Susquehanna last summer as a rising senior. But he didn't receive an offer to return after graduation. “Just because you've got an internship offer at one place and have seen that big paycheck, it doesn't mean you've made it,” he says. The disappointment didn't last long; Shah landed a full-time job offer from another firm a couple of weeks ago. Still, his highs and lows underscore how precarious these ultracompetitive internship programs can be. Even for those who are highly skilled at making predictions, the surest bet is that you'll be humbled eventually.

title: Nicotine Undergoes a Rebrand
dek: The following items first appeared in Sara Ashley O'Brien's weekly Wellness newsletter
body_en:
The rebranding of nicotine is well underway. Influencers and entrepreneurs are spreading the idea that the highly addictive substance can actually be good for you in small doses. They're claiming it can improve attention span, mood and memory. Companies promoting tobacco-free nicotine products are leaning in to health, wellness and fitness associations, too.

Lucy, which sells “intelligent nicotine” products, including flavored gum and pouches, states on its website that “whether you use nicotine to enhance focus, boost your energy, or relax—there's a Lucy perfect for you.” Athletic Nicotine's website features a young woman on a rowing machine with text that reads: “Next-level nicotine for the winner in all of us.” Another brand, Nic Nac, touts “premium ingredients” and tells consumers to use its lozenges “anywhere you need an edge, whether it's in the gym, office, or on an airplane.”

The companies each told me that their products are intended for existing adult nicotine consumers. Athletic Nicotine said it does not market itself “as a health product, wellness supplement, or performance enhancer.” Lucy said that its website copy is meant to appeal to people who are already using nicotine for those purposes.

Pull quote: “Influencers are spreading the idea nicotine can actually be good in small doses. Research debunks claims.”

For years, influencers have been talking about nicotine as a wellness product. They've promoted smoke-free nicotine formulations including lozenges, pouches and gums. It's a familiar phenomenon in the era of D.I.Y. health: Influencers using anecdotal evidence and limited research to peddle the next holy-grail product. Their talking points can have powerful ripple effects for their followings. While nicotine products like pouches are deemed less harmful than cigarettes—which harm nearly every organ of the body—the substance is what makes tobacco products so addictive.

The pulmonologist Dr. Hasmeena Kathuria penned a column in the Washington Post recently debunking wellness claims about nicotine and underscoring its risks. She writes that nicotine activates the body's fight-or-flight response, increases heart rate and blood pressure and can disrupt sleep.

Researchers haven't found an association between cognition and nicotine use, Melissa Little, an associate professor of public-health sciences at the University of Virginia—my alma mater—told me. She's also director of the school's Center for Nicotine & Tobacco Research. “The evidence on the benefits of nicotine on memory, mood and metabolism is not well supported,” she said. She added that any mood improvements findings from nicotine use are primarily from “smokers who use nicotine replacement to manage withdrawal symptoms. Most nonsmokers find nicotine worsens their mood and even increases nausea.” Plus, the long-term health effects of nicotine products like pouches are still unknown, she said.

Meanwhile, sales of nicotine pouches increased by 319% between January 2023 and May 2026.

title: Facial fat grafting grows
dek: Item from Sara Ashley O'Brien's weekly Wellness newsletter
body_en:
My colleague Chavie Lieber and I published an article recently about how facial filler has fallen out of favor. The filler look—characterized by overly plump lips and pillowy cheeks—is losing appeal. It's partly because people are shrinking due to GLP-1s, so their features, too, must scale to size.

The American Society of Plastic Surgeons recently released its annual report with statistics showing cosmetic-procedure trends in 2025. Notably, 82% of the organization's member surgeons reported receiving consultation requests related to GLP-1 use in 2025. Of all cosmetic procedures tracked, one saw the most growth year-over-year: facial fat grafting.

Facial fat grafting, up 39% in 2025 compared with the year prior, involves removing fat from elsewhere in the body, such as the stomach, via liposuction and then having it injected into the face. The idea is to rejuvenate and restore lost volume, which might come as a result of weight loss. “Ozempic Face” isn't what most people are going for when they start taking these medications. The desired outcome is a more naturally filled out look.

“People want to look as good as they feel,” ASPS president Dr. Bob Basu, a plastic surgeon in Houston, told me. “People want to look refreshed, but they want to look like an authentic version of themselves, and I think that's where fat comes into play.”

ASPS said it no longer reports the costs of procedures because they're variable, fluctuating by many factors including geographic location or a surgeon's expertise. In 2024, the organization said the price for the surgeon's fee for facial fat grafting was between $3,000 and $5,500, which doesn't include additional costs for things like anesthesia, operating room facility fees and other fees.

Dr. Kelly Killeen, an ASPS member and plastic surgeon at the Practice Healthcare in Beverly Hills, told me facial fat grafting can even sometimes be done in the office, depending on how much fat is being placed and any other procedures involved. She said it could run from as little as $4,000 up to more than $20,000, with add-ons like skin-tightening procedures.

title: Videos of People Paying Down Their Debt Are Generating Interest
dek: Viewers return to cheer, judge and see whether balances went up or down
body_en:
Facing your debt can be painful. Watching someone else deal with theirs can be gripping. That became clear to Rodney Morgan in July, when he posted a TikTok of himself sitting on a blowup mattress with his head in one hand, and his debt tally of $40,058.44 imposed on the screen.

“I'm rebuilding from scratch as a flight attendant and being honest about where I'm starting,” wrote Morgan, a 33-year-old Los Angeles resident. It was a changeup from his usual posts about life as a flight attendant, and racked up 1.5 million views—far more than the roughly 100,000 views he said his previous best-performing videos drew.

TikTok is filled with influencers dispensing all manner of advice on how to get ahead financially, whether it is saving to retire early, earning a passive income or using credit-card rewards to fund a globe-trotting lifestyle. But users are also finding big audiences showing the private money struggles many would be too embarrassed to share.

The format is simple: Users share the exact amount they owe, along with updates on how they are chipping away at the figure—or suffering setbacks. Viewers tune in to see the numbers move up and down and root for people, often weighing in with advice.

More than 28,000 debt-related videos were uploaded to TikTok in the 12 months through September, according to Tubular Labs, which tracks social-video viewing.

Part of #DebtTok's draw is that it addresses a taboo topic that people feel they can't discuss even with friends and family. Like gossip, the videos let viewers size up other people's financial choices and measure their own against them, said Brooke Erin Duffy, a Cornell University professor who studies social-media culture.

Personal-finance gurus like Suze Orman and Dave Ramsey gained huge followings by dispensing advice to callers who shared their money problems. TikTok videos cut out the guru—the host is the person with the problem, not the one giving advice.

Viewers tune in for the drama of a hero's journey, like a movie where someone takes on a big obstacle, said Brittney Castro, a certified financial planner at Chime, a mobile banking app. “It's so human to want to see that person win and succeed,” she said.

For those posting about their debt, racking up views can help pay off bills. TikTok pays creators for some popular videos, and viewers can send virtual gifts during livestreams. Creators also earn income when brands sponsor their posts, or a cut when followers buy through links they share.

After Morgan's video took off, for instance, a personal-finance app offered him his biggest social-media deal yet. He expects the sponsored post to pay off a piece of his debt: the roughly $800 left on the Home Depot and Lowe's cards he opened to remodel his house.

Every night before bed, Tianna Carter records an update on her debt, sometimes at 10 p.m. in her kitchen. “I look forward to it every day,” she said. Carter, a 31-year-old human-resources director for a public school district, didn't say at first the amount she owed: $54,057.93. Then she decided to share the figure. “People understand more and can relate more to my number,” said Carter, who lives in Harrisburg, Pa. Her followers don't always agree with her choices, such as her spending on her personal upkeep. “How am I supposed to keep you accountable if you're getting your hair done?” one commenter wrote. Carter said she treats salon visits as fixed costs and cuts elsewhere, like bringing lunch to work. She puts the money she makes from her posts toward daycare costs and paying down her debt.

When Kayla Rose was in college, her father gave her a credit card for groceries and gas. She ended up using it to buy clothes, workout gear and home décor as well, promoting some of what she bought in her videos. Rose, now a 29-year-old full-time influencer in Palm Beach, Fla., told followers in March that she owed more than $25,000 on credit cards and planned to pay it off with money she made from her videos. The posts about her debt brought new followers, and she paid off the cards in August. “What paid off my credit-card debt was these silly little videos you guys are currently watching,” she told followers.

title: Lights, Camera, Costumes!
dek: As silent movies emerged as an art form, fashion played an essential, energizing role on screen
body_en:
New York. The story for Paramount's 1927 silent movie “It” was provided by the British writer Elinor Glyn, who used the word to mean a “magnetic force” that draws others. The 21-year-old actress Clara Bow, who starred in the film, was henceforth known as the first “It Girl.” Charisma? Glamour? Not quite. Her creamy cheeks, tousled bob and bright, beguiling eyes brought a hint of id, jolts of energy, into the picture. And energy was what moving pictures were all about. Where photographs were still, and theater could talk, silent movies were action and “It” was everything.

That the mute infant art form soon relied on fashions that excited the eye should come as no surprise. Glyn's older sister, Lady Duff-Gordon, otherwise known as the couturier Lucile, immediately forged relationships with actresses—Billie Burke, for instance. As early as 1913 she was designing heart-stopping gowns for their movies, which in turn brought renown to her fashion house. What is surprising is that “Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film,” at New York's Bard Graduate Center, is the first major exhibition to explore the subject.

Launched in the U.S. in 1896, with the New York premiere of Thomas Edison's Vitascope film projector, silent movies astonished audiences. And yet the medium, entirely visual, posed definite challenges. “Seeking ways to craft narratives without audible dialogue,” reads the show's introductory wall text, “filmmakers used costume to convey character, drive plot, and heighten emotion.”

The first costumes were made by dressmakers and couturiers, but a network of costume professionals would emerge, designers who realized that clothing in film had to be fascinating, energized—stories within the story.

The show's co-organizers—Michelle Finamore, a fashion and design historian, and Emma Cormack, the associate curator for exhibitions and study collection curator at Bard Graduate Center—remind us that during those early decades, when the movie industry began on the East Coast, and relocated to California in the mid-1910s, costumes were not preserved. Even after the advent of the talkies, and well into the sound era, they were reused and revised with no thought to historical value. Leslie Caron once told me that the unforgettable white gown she wore in 1958's “Gigi,” designed by Cecil Beaton and ravishing with swallow's wings at the shoulders, was used on and on, feathers plucked, and that it eventually had sleeves. Garments that have lasted, usually aided by conservation, are rare—and rarely exhibited.

So it's quite the bounty that the exhibition presents 16 surviving silent-screen treasures along with stills and film clips that show the pieces in action. Among them are two ensembles worn by Lillian Gish in D.W. Griffith's “Way Down East” (1920); a risqué Travis Banton evening dress used in both Dorothy Arzner's “Fashions for Women” (1927) and A. Edward Sutherland's “Pointed Heels” (1929); and a fringed mauve gown from which Gloria Swanson unwound herself in Cecil B. DeMille's “Male and Female” (1919). These gems are surrounded by a wealth of period garments, accessories, artworks, posters, sketches, photographs and clips from over 50 silent movies.

The exhibition of more than 180 objects unfolds over three floors, with the first bringing us into the early moviegoing experience. A 1920s usher's uniform in sky blue with black trim, likely from the Plaza Theatre in London, stands at the entrance. Videos show people at the new “picture palaces,” where genders and classes mingle and comic clashes ensue. Displays of brightly colored glass preview slides, fanzines such as Photoplay, and Beautebox tins lithographed with the faces of stars (Pola Negri! Bebe Daniels!) illustrate the various forms of advertising and collectibles aimed at filmgoers.

On the second floor, the curators look at the actresses who went to Callot Soeurs, Madame Frances and Henri Bendel for their costumes, and then move on to the new studio system and its designers, who pulled a sense of color from the black-and-white spectrum, and exploited reflective materials—lamé, panné velvet, satin, sequins—for onscreen shimmer and flash. Silent movies may be the home of slapstick, but they are also akin to ballet. Light reinforces gesture and shadows contour expression.

On the third floor, the focus is movement, “woven into the fabric of cinema” through dance-hall and jazz-club settings, as well as in scenes of driving, swimming, riding and piloting. A surprisingly immaculate canary-yellow dress, glitteringly embellished for Mae Murray in “Circe the Enchantress” (1924), is flanked by the film that has her wearing it in a nightclub, dancing up a storm. Look at those Watteau straps in the back, dripping with rhinestones and looping, swinging, amplifying the dynamics. Onscreen the dress is the color of limelight.

With precise plotting and symbolic pieces, the curators have neatly fit the era into the center's jewel-box spaces. Nothing is belabored. And who would have guessed that a grail of It-ness would be part of the show, nestled next to the matador jacket worn by Rudolph Valentino in 1922's “Blood and Sand.” On loan from La Cinémathèque Française, Paris, laid flat in a vitrine, is a flesh-colored silk-chiffon slip dress, its hem beaded with silver lozenges. A relic from “Red Hair,” a 1928 silent film now lost, it was made for Clara Bow.

Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film. Bard Graduate Center, through Jan. 3, 2027.

Ms. Jacobs is the Arts Intel Report editor for the newsletter Air Mail.

title: How the AI Boom Ends
body_en:
I can tell you how the artificial-intelligence data-center boom will probably end, but I can't tell you when. Implementing large language models has been a brute-force approach: Big, fast and expensive GPUs from Nvidia crunch a trillion parameters using massive amounts of memory housed in liquid-cooled, gigawatt-gobbling data centers, all with brute-force pricing. It sure smells like IBM mainframes of old.

Be careful about extrapolating anything from today's pricing. With AI, like all new technologies, the refinement stage is kicking in—just as mainframes gave way to cheaper minicomputers, microprocessors, web servers and now AI architectures. AI token prices have been dropping but are set to plunge faster than most anticipate. Tech growth is never a straight line.

Silicon Valley's mantra for decades has been smaller, cheaper, faster, better. I asked venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson to translate that into numbers. “We often see a technology shift when the new approach is 10 times better. It can be 10 times more performant or 10 times cheaper, sometimes both.” He calls it the “factor of 10.”

And it's happening. Last week, according to OpenRouter, OpenAI and Anthropic were charging a premium for some of their models—$1 to $2 per million input tokens. Comparable Chinese open-weight models like Z.ai's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen charged 6 to 12 cents, around 90% less—that factor of 10 inflection point. American AI labs have gone from 70% market share last year to 30% today. All are still growing. But prices matter.

AI architecture is evolving. Instead of a trillion parameters, efficient small language models might use 70 billion and run on an Apple Mac. These local models have no token costs beyond the cost of hardware and electricity. But they must be less capable than the large language models, right? Not really. Stanford researchers show that a locally run small language model “can successfully answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries.”

No question we'll always have high-end models running in data centers. IBM still sells mainframes. But growth will happen elsewhere. Where? Another Silicon Valley saying I've lived by: Intelligence moves out to the edge of the network. The real breakthrough will happen when robust AI models run on smartphones. It's already starting. In September, California-based PrismML released a compressed version of the popular open-source Qwen3.8 27B AI model. The company got it down to under 6 gigabytes. That means it fits not only on PCs but also on high-end smartphones. The memory size is reduced by roughly 9 to 10 times. There's that factor of 10.

Technology doesn't stand still. Qualcomm recently announced a new Snapdragon neural processing unit, or NPU, for smartphones. Using what the company calls a “mixture-of-experts” model, it could run a 30 billion parameter AI model in 3 gigabytes of memory. According to the Deep View, the largest AI model on a phone has been four billion parameters on an Apple A20 Pro chip. Qualcomm provides a 7.5 times boost.

Demand isn't about to let up, but prices will start plunging by factors of 10.

NPUs, like Qualcomm's new Snapdragon and Google's Tensor chips in its Pixel phones, are multiplying. Same for the latest Apple M- and A-series chips, engines that can run AI models locally on iPhones—maybe why Apple hasn't joined the AI data-center spending delirium.

A Nvidia-backed startup, Reflection AI, claims it matches leading Chinese open-weight AI models with “3-4x less inference compute.” That's it? Only 3 or 4 times? Wake me up when it's 10 times. At the pace AI is moving, that could be year-end.

Agents are all the rage, from Meta's Muse to xAI's Grokbot. They run on virtual machines in data centers but raise all sorts of privacy concerns. Startup Perplexity recently teamed up with Nvidia to run agents on PCs. Zero token costs. And you own your data.

I often hear, that if tokens get cheaper, demand will go up. That's Jevons Paradox. Sure, elasticity works. But if prices drop 90%, demand must increase 900% just to stay flat. Remember when internet demand grew while debt-laden Global Crossing spectacularly failed because prices dropped too fast? Historically, semiconductors got 30% cheaper every year. When prices dropped by more than 50%, disaster struck with fabrication plant closings and company failures.

Will 2027 see peak data center? Again, timing is dicey. Current demand is gangbusters, but spending is a game of chicken until multiple factor-of-10 improvements kick in and prices collapse. This could set off a cascade of data-center halts and debt defaults, even as token demand increases.

Yes, model training, drug discovery and winning prizes like the recently solved Navier-Stokes equations require hot chips in data centers. But chatbots and agents and other tasks may increasingly be handled on PCs and phones and smart glasses and whatever new gizmos Silicon Valley invents over the next decade.

I've heard this called the “Great Migration.” Mr. Jurvetson's factor of 10 is visible now, as it often is, but ignored. Change doesn't happen overnight. It happens gradually, then suddenly.

title: Fusionism
dek: An Alliance Of Principles. Book: “Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right” by Stephanie Slade (Notre Dame, 304 pages, $30)
body_en:
The name of Frank Meyer is rarely heard on the political right today. Younger conservatives in the 2020s won't know much about fusionism, the political outlook Meyer formulated—briefly, the idea that free markets, virtue and tradition can cohere with one another. Since his death in 1972, fusionism's heyday, it has gone out of fashion, replaced by a form of right-wing bellicosity with little patience for compromise.

Stephanie Slade's “Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right” explores the intellectual roots of fusionism and, by extension, American conservatism. The starting point is the great debate between traditionalists as defenders of order, morality, religion and virtue, and libertarians and classical liberals as advocates of the free market and individual rights. Over time, neither side achieved dominance within American conservatism; what emerged instead was a “fusion” of the two. Ms. Slade, an editor at Reason magazine, has given us an excellent account of a once-influential political outlook that deserves renewed attention.

Fusionism was given its first full expression in the Sharon Statement of 1960, drafted by young conservatives in the home of William F. Buckley Jr. in Sharon, Conn. They believed conservatives needed a solid philosophical and metaphysical foundation anchored in the principles of limited government, free markets and individual rights. For them, liberty and virtue were the two pillars on which any good society rests. We need freedom to be virtuous, the fusionists argued, and we require virtue to live happily and freely. “The task of the conservative movement in America,” Ms. Slade explains, “was to ‘harmonize’ social conservatism with free-market economics . . . because human flourishing is impossible without freedom as well as virtue.”

Fusionists were liberals, but their liberalism differed from that of the progressives. This is evident in their conception of the role of the state. In the fusionist view, the state can't be trusted with authority over economic, moral, religious or lifestyle questions. Its job is to keep individuals free so that they can pursue a life of virtue on their own. Fusionists were conservatives, but their traditionalism had little in common with the vision of ultraconservatives who opposed the values of the modern world.

Fusionism, Ms. Slade maintains, was not merely an alliance between factions for short-term political gain. It offered a coherent set of shared commitments with a pedigree that runs through the American founding. Russell Kirk and Friedrich Hayek held views that seem irreconcilable, but they both adhered more closely to fusionist principles than is commonly understood. The same goes for Milton Friedman, who remained in the fusionist orbit for a long time.

Another arguably fusionist figure discussed in the book is Ronald Reagan, who combined libertarian leanings with genuine appreciation for freedom anchored in virtue. Sadly, Reagan's worldview has fallen into disrepute among what Ms. Slade calls the Dissident Right. She devotes half of the book to an analysis of the current political landscape on the right and explains why Reagan's vision is deeply at odds with today's scorched-earth politics.

Pull quote: “A half-century ago, conservatives championed free markets and moral traditionalism. Much of today's right has abandoned that synthesis.”

How did the Republican Party go from Reagan to Donald Trump? Today's right-wing populism, Ms. Slade asserts, has roots in the post-Reagan years when a split emerged between neoconservatives, committed to free markets and global cooperation, and paleoconservatives, who embraced economic nationalism, protectionism and anti-immigrant policies. The latter hearkened back to an earlier America First isolationism and introduced coarseness into political debates, vilifying adversaries and dissidents within their own camp. In Ms. Slade's assessment, the face of the paleocon movement was “Pitchfork Pat” Buchanan, whose militant and isolationist worldview reached its maturity in the MAGA movement. “The paleocons were concerned less with keeping the government small,” she writes, “than with ensuring it be used to promote the right causes and help the right people.”

Six decades ago, Meyer worried that a heresy had crept into Republican thinking, one that demanded election victories at all costs and that placed no importance on principle or policy. If he were alive today, he would not be pleased with his friends. The Dissident Right exploits grievance and status resentments triggered by immigration and economic hardship. Its leaders declare opponents traitors and denounce compromise, gradualism and moderation as signs of weakness. The Dissident Right, Ms. Slade persuasively shows, believes that our system of checks and balances and limited government is rotten and must give way to a “Caesarist” approach to executive power. Self-described conservatives jettison free-market policies and embrace big deficits and government expenditures for the benefit of Republican voting constituencies; their aim isn't to shrink the state or limit its purview but to control and expand it for nakedly partisan purposes.

Could an updated form of fusionism ameliorate some of these pathologies? Nobody knows for sure. Breathing life into the liberty-virtue synthesis might require relinquishing the vocabulary of fusionism. Perhaps a new type of conservatism will emerge that reflects and responds to the complexity and tensions of modern life.

Ms. Slade believes that there is a kernel of fusionism in almost all of us. She may be right. It is impossible, in the 21st century, to identify a single overriding interest or value that ought alone to govern social life, whether freedom, virtue, equality or efficiency. During the Cold War, as collectivism made advances in all areas of life, individualism made sense as a lodestar. But we live in a multiplicity of realms—social, economic, cultural, political, religious—that follow their own logic and cannot be reduced to a single principle. What's needed is a balance between rival values and principles that is flexible, moderate and resistant to doctrinal purity. Ms. Slade's history of fusionism might help conservatives practice this art of balance in dark times.

Mr. Craiutu is a professor of political science at Indiana University, Bloomington.

title: What Are U.S. Soldiers Doing in Ecuador?
body_en:
News that U.S. soldiers were deployed to Ecuador last month to fight drug-trafficking cartels deserves more attention than it has received. A trademark pledge of President Trump is to stay out of “endless wars.” Yet if ever there were a conflict destined to go on forever, it's the armed effort to defeat the suppliers of mind-altering substances in the face of robust consumer demand.

This isn't to dismiss out of hand the Shield of the Americas, the new U.S. regional security initiative under which the Ecuador mission was launched. The State Department says the goal of the hemispheric project, unveiled in March, is to pull together “likeminded allies” to “work together to advance strategies that stop foreign interference in our hemisphere, criminal and narco-terrorist gangs and cartels, and illegal and mass immigration.”

Enhanced cooperation on the security interests of pro-Western countries in the hemisphere is a welcome development. To the extent it's possible for the U.S. to assist neighbors in recovering democratic institutions that have been lost to organized crime, the initiative has promise. But if the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, operating under the “shield,” requires sending American soldiers to fight in the jungles of far-flung lands, it will tread on dangerous ground.

The U.S. successfully supported Colombia and President Álvaro Uribe in that country's war against narco-trafficking rebels in the 2000s by helping with intelligence, equipment and training and by sending in military advisers. It never committed troops.

A growing number of countries now welcome security help from the U.S. because armed groups have overwhelmed national police and military. The problems go well beyond narcotics production and trafficking. Criminal networks rule swaths of weak countries. They run extortion and kidnapping rackets, collect taxes, interfere with elections, traffic people, intimidate the political class with threats of violence, and run illegal gold-mining operations that trample the rights of mining companies and rural communities.

Quito is one of 19 governments that have joined the shield. Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Peru and Panama are members. Four Caribbean countries, including the Dominican Republic, are in the group. Most member governments are center-right. Guatemala is one notable exception. All have reason to worry about threats to democracy from transnational criminal networks.

Over the past decade drug traffickers searching for the path of least resistance from South America to the north have gravitated to Ecuador. Once a small-bore banana republic marked by political instability, its weak institutions, rampant corruption and attractive location made it a target for gangsters looking to create a transit hub. It is now an organized-crime hot spot.

Quito wants help in curbing cartel violence, but demand for drugs persists. As cartel violence has intensified and security has deteriorated, Ecuadorians have desperately sought a way back to the old tranquility they remember. President Daniel Noboa won a special election in 2023 and a regular election in 2025 by promising to crack down on crime. But progress has been slow. The arrival of U.S. forces raised hopes that the tide will soon turn. In raids last month, Ecuadorian forces, fighting alongside Americans, killed three alleged narcos and captured dozens more.

Yet the broader strategy is unclear. Mr. Uribe's triumph in Colombia over the guerrillas and the paramilitary didn't end the flow of cocaine to the U.S. One reason is that American demand for narcotics is inelastic: Even when the white hats reduce supply and prices go up, consumers keep buying. The net effect is that cartel income increases.

Illicit groups aren't about to abandon their profitable businesses. But they can be cut down to size. The difficulty is finding a way to minimize their capacity to control territory without trampling republican values. Mr. Uribe managed that. His government re-established its authority across the country and restored it to its proper function of defending life and property without destroying democracy. Contrast that with El Salvador, which has gone the strongman route, employing high-powered weapons and sweeping lockups with no due process and at the expense of pluralism. Freedom has been exchanged for peace. Some political opponents of President Nayib Bukele have fled into exile. Sadly, the Trump administration celebrates Mr. Bukele.

Ecuador could come out a winner if it can copy Colombia and avoid the error of El Salvador. If the costs of operating in Ecuador go high enough, gangsters might even leave, establishing routes through different countries. It's what regional analysts call the “balloon effect.” The trouble is it doesn't do much for the Americas. To reach a lasting peace, the region will do better to emphasize open markets, deregulation, transparency, independent institutions that check the concentration of power, and efforts to professionalize the military. That's a hemispheric cause worth fighting for.

Write to O'Grady@wsj.com.

title: Will the FTC Protect You From Discounts?
body_en:
The Federal Trade Commission seems poised to join the backlash against personalized pricing. That would be a mistake. The practice remains poorly understood.

Personalized pricing, or its more sinister name, “surveillance pricing,” is a method of setting prices whereby companies use personal data to make individualized offers. According to a new FTC proposal, personalized pricing likely constitutes an “unfair or deceptive” practice unless the seller discloses “the fact that the price is personalized, the basis of that personalization, and the type of data used.”

The agency's conclusion is premature and relies on incomplete information. Don't take my word for it. The FTC concedes as much, stating in its August enforcement bulletin that “the extent to which businesses currently use personalized pricing is not well understood, and the effects of personalized pricing on consumers are unclear.”

Nor do we have a grasp of its prevalence. Remarkably, the FTC's proposal doesn't cite a single instance of a company's using personalized pricing.

The commission rushes to regulate personalized pricing.

Rather, it relies on hypotheticals designed to make the practice appear harmful to consumers. Consider a grocery chain charging more for milk to a family with children. A hotel could charge a higher price for a person traveling for a funeral. These scenarios strain credulity. The FTC should develop its enforcement policy around real-world behavior, not imagined harms.

According to the theory of perfect price discrimination, a monopolist charges each consumer the maximum price that he is willing to pay for a good or service. This would make consumers worse off because all the gains from trade go to the seller.

In reality, even a monopolist wouldn't be able to extract all consumer surplus, because of the presence of alternatives and the inability to fully know consumers' willingness to pay. With personalized pricing, some buyers would see higher prices and others lower ones. The overall effect on consumer welfare is an empirical question.

So far, only one study, from 2022, has directly examined it with a pricing field experiment. Researchers at the University of Chicago found personalized pricing could benefit many consumers. While the practice raised prices for some, 60% were better off. They received individualized offers that were lower than the previous uniform price.

These results should give the FTC reason to pause any proposed enforcement and first develop a better understanding of personalized pricing. Instead of caricaturing how firms set prices, the commission should grapple with how the practice actually works. Rather than assume personalized pricing is always bad for consumers, it should account for the possible benefits suggested by scholars. Our limited knowledge provides little justification for rushing forward with policies that could effectively ban personalized pricing—a practice whose potential upside we have yet to fully understand.

Ms. Sullivan, a former FTC economist, is a visiting scholar at the George Washington University Regulatory Studies Center.

title: Trump’s Diesel Insult to Lindsey Graham
body_en:
The world misses Lindsey Graham, and never more than now as President Trump sides more decidedly with Vladimir Putin in his war against Ukraine and Europe. The late Senator might have been able to persuade the President to avoid this moral and strategic mistake.

Mr. Trump announced late Friday that the U.S. will buy up to 4.8 million tons (nearly 36 million barrels) of Russian diesel fuel in stages. That includes an “immediate” supply of 300,000 tons, another 500,000 in November, and one million “immediately thereafter.”

The delivery of another three million tons is “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries,” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. The U.S. Treasury lifted some sanctions on Russia through April 7 so it could export the diesel.

“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

This is supposed to help Republicans in the November elections that are three weeks away. But 36 million barrels of Russian diesel won't move prices much. The world consumed 28 million barrels of diesel and other distillates daily in 2025, according to OPIS, which is part of Dow Jones Energy.

What the deal will do is directly finance Mr. Putin's bloody war in Ukraine. And it may be worse. The Financial Times reported Saturday that the Trump Administration “threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing” to Kyiv if it continues attacking Russian refineries.

In September Mr. Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel-fuel shortages with its long-range strikes on Russian refineries. Never mind Iranian and Houthi strikes on Middle Eastern energy production and transport. Russia helps Iran with intelligence and weapons.

On Sunday Mr. Trump announced what he called “an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine supports such a cease-fire if Russia does the same, but as we write this Russia hasn't commented.

An energy cease-fire would help both sides, as Ukraine faces another harsh winter and Russian refineries are under siege. But what about Mr. Putin's relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities?

His deal with Putin helps the Kremlin's war on Ukraine's cities.

On Wednesday 22 people, including five children, were killed in a Russian cruise missile strike on an apartment building in the city of Pryluky. The next day a glide bomb hit two buses in Kramatorsk, killing 33. After the diesel announcement, Russia launched glide bombs Saturday at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20, including three children. Without a complete cease-fire, Russia will continue to torment Ukrainian civilians.

The strategic turn here is hard to understand. Only last month Mr. Trump signed Lindsey Graham's bill to allow new sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. Now Mr. Trump has decided to buy Russian diesel and lift some current U.S. sanctions. The U.S. has been browbeating Europe, India and China not to buy Russian oil, and so much for all that diplomatic effort.

The Kremlin has been under financial pressure from Western sanctions and Ukraine's ability to hit targets in Russia. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates Russian oil companies will earn some $4.5 billion from the diesel deal.

Mr. Trump added to the pressure on Ukraine by saying it's “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” But he'll have to search far and wide for anyone in Ukraine who supports financing Vladimir Putin.

Mr. Trump complained again on the weekend that Mr. Zelensky could have settled the war many times. Yes, Kyiv could always surrender. Ukrainians prefer to fight for their independence and freedom. Eyeing a Nobel peace prize, Mr. Trump wants to broker a Russia-Ukraine peace, but the only pressure he ever applies is on Ukraine.

His multiple attempts at appeasing Mr. Putin with summitry, flattery, offers of new investment, and more haven't moved the Russian. On the weekend a Russian official said the diesel deal doesn't change Mr. Putin's determination to achieve his war aim, which is to turn Ukraine into a Kremlin satrapy. Until that changes, Mr. Trump's diesel deal helps Russia and not the cause of peace.

title: How to Make a Jihadist Martyr
body_en:
Jihadist killer Nidal Hasan deserves his future in hell, but before he gets there Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wants him to die before a firing squad open to the public for all to watch and record. This is a bad idea for many reasons, not least that it offers the killer the public martyrdom he craves.

These columns don't oppose the death penalty. For some murders, it shows that a society is serious enough about its self-preservation to deliver retributive justice. Mr. Hasan killed 13 and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood in 2009 in the name of Islam.

But his execution is best done quietly with few witnesses beyond officials and the families of the victims who wish to attend. This consigns him to history with ignominy but no fanfare. Mr. Hasan has said “I would still be a martyr” if executed, and that he killed those soldiers because they were “going against the Islamic Empire.” A livestreamed death, complete with some incendiary last words, is what he wants.

Mr. Hegseth seems to think a livestreamed execution by firing squad will be a show of U.S. resolve and deter others from such murderous acts. This misjudges the jihadist mind. It is a miscalculation that Western leaders often make about revolutionary jihadists like those who now run Iran.

Mr. Hasan and his ilk understand they are likely to die. That is part of their fevered calculation. They imagine that by their violence they will contribute to the bloody caliphate they hope to build on earth.

A public death by firing squad would give Mr. Hasan that publicity in perpetuity. It would assist the cult of death promoted by the perversion of Islam seeking to recruit more suicide attackers. Far from deterring jihadists, it would serve as a YouTube recruiting video.

The U.S. doesn't need to execute Mr. Hasan on live TV to send a deterrent message. It needs to win the war against jihadists around the world, which at the moment means the fight against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its Houthi allies. If this weekend's attack on Riyadh is a guide, Mr. Hegseth has more urgent duties on that front.

title: Democrats vs. Alaska, Again
body_en:
The Alaska Senate race is a toss-up this year, which is remarkable given how Democrats in Washington keep demonstrating their zeal to stop economic development in the state. They did it again before they left town last month, blocking a bill that would have aided oil and gas development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR).

In 2017 Congress required the Interior Secretary to create a plan for developing oil and gas in the ANWR coastal plain with a competitive program for leasing, developing and transporting the resources. The Biden Administration quickly suspended the leases in 2021 pending environmental review. Joe Biden's Interior Secretary later canceled the leases. The political seesaw left developers without enough confidence in stable policy to make the large investments required to get the region's rich reserves out of the ground.

Trump II has opened more development leases for bidding, but companies are understandably wary of investing in projects that can be shut down by the next Democratic administration. In June the Bureau of Land Management's ANWR lease sale offered some 689,000 acres for lease but received bids on about 70,000 acres, worth about $3.7 million.

Enter Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, who proposed to provide some federal assurance that the leases can't be canceled by the stroke of a pen. The Alaska's Right to Produce Act 2.0 would have prevented leases in the coastal plain oil and gas leasing program from being canceled unless the lessee is in violation of the lease terms.

Democrats and the climate lobby blocked it from getting a vote on the Senate floor. Defenders of Wildlife said the bill would produce “rampant oil and gas drilling,” while Sen. Martin Heinrich (D., N.M.) called it “another bill that would prioritize oil and gas over literally everything else.”

That's odd, since New Mexico is a major oil and gas producing state and Mr. Heinrich's constituents profit from it. The U.S. Energy Information Administration says New Mexico had 4.15 trillion cubic feet of gross natural gas withdrawals in 2025, far more than Alaska.

Pull quote: “They vote to keep oil and gas in the ground in a state that needs jobs and investment.”

Opponents say oil and gas leases in ANWR would destroy wildlife habitats, spoil the wilderness and infringe on sacred indigenous lands. But no one is proposing to pave the Arctic. If all of the 2026 leases offered had been purchased, the less than 700,000 acres would have been a small fraction of the more than 19 million acre wildlife refuge.

Progressives want Alaska to be a nature preserve for tourism and dog-sled races. But the oil industry makes up a significant portion of Alaska's GDP, and future oil and gas leases will add jobs and tax revenue. It also serves America's energy needs and national-security interests. Across his two terms, Sen. Sullivan has been a champion for bringing investment to a state that needs more of both, while protecting the environment.

His opponent, Mary Peltola, initially co-sponsored a version of this legislation when she was in the U.S. House. When the vote took place on the floor, she voted “present.” Ms. Peltola could provide the 51st vote to give Democrats a majority, and then vote “present” to put even more of Alaska's vast energy resources in a deep political freeze.
